### What does the acronym IR mean?

- [ ] Internet Ranking
- [x] Information Retrieval
- [ ] Indexed Repository
- [ ] Intelligent Reasoning

> Explanation:
> IR means **Information Retrieval**, term created by Calvin N. Moors in 1950.
> It refers to the discipline of automatically finding relevant information in large collections of documents.




---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### Who invented the term "Information Retrieval" and in what year?

- [ ] Gerard Salton, 1968
- [ ] Hans Peter Luhn, 1959
- [x] Calvin N. Moors, 1950
- [ ] Maron and Kuhns, 1960

> Explanation:
> **Calvin N. Moors** coined the term *Information Retrieval* in **1950**, marking the official birth of the discipline.
> Luhn (1959) described statistical recovery, Maron and Kuhns (1960) defined the probabilistic model.




---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### What is a zettabyte (zetabyte)?

- [ ] $2^{10}$ bytes
- [ ] 1 million terabytes
- [x] $2^{70}$ bytes, or 1 billion terabytes
- [ ] $2^{50}$ bytes

> Explanation:
> One **zettabyte** = $2^{70}$ bytes = **1 billion terabytes**.
> This is the unit used to measure the global production of digital data, which exceeded 180 zettabytes in 2025.




---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### What proportion of online time was spent on research (Searches) in 2012?

- [ ] 5 %
- [ ] 13%
- [ ] 19%
- [x] 21 %

> Explanation:
> In 2012, **21%** of online time was spent on research.
> By combining research (21%) and content reading (20%), we reach **41%** of online time directly related to access to information activities.




---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### Which of these elements is NOT a direct application of distance measurement in IR?

- [ ] Document clustering
- [ ] Classification by k-NN
- [ ] Reduction of dimensionality
- [x] File Compression

> Explanation:
> **File compression** is not an IR distance measurement application.
> On the other hand, clustering, k-NN classification and dimensionality reduction are all based on measurements of distance or similarity between documents.




---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### The growth in the volume of global digital data is of the following nature:

- [ ] Linear
- [ ] Logarithmic
- [x] exponential
- [ ] Constant

> Explanation:
> Growth is **exponential**: from 2 zettabytes in 2010 to over 180 in 2025.
> This acceleration is due to the multiplication of data sources (smartphones, IoT, social networks, streaming...).




---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### True or False: The Cranfield (1966) project defined the first evaluation measures in IR.

- [x] True
- [ ] False

> Explanation:
> **Real.** The Cranfield project introduced the measures of **precision** (Precision) and **recall** (Recall) in 1966, which remain fundamental in IR today.
> This is the first project to evaluate IR systems in a rigorous and comparative manner.




---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### True or False: Dense Embedding places the majority of its coordinates at zero.

- [ ] True
- [x] False

> Explanation:
> **False.** The **embeddings hollow** (Sparse Embeddings) have the majority of their coordinates at zero (a document uses only a small subset of the total vocabulary).
> The **denses** (Dense Embeddings) have all their non-zero coordinates and are learned by neural networks.




---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### What is the order of the steps in the information management pipeline?

- [x] Raw documents → Extracting features → Mapping → Representation space → User interaction → Decision
- [ ] Decision → Raw documents → Mapping → User interaction
- [ ] User interaction → Raw documents → Extraction → Decision
- [ ] Mapping → Raw documents → Extraction → Representation

> Explanation:
> The pipeline always follows this order:
> ** raw documents** (Raw Documents) → **Extraction of features** (Feature Extraction) → **Mapping** → **Representation space** → **User interaction** → **Decision**.
> This is the core of the information management process.




---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### What is the fundamental difference between hollow embeddeding (Sparse) and dense embeddeding (Dense)?

- [ ] Hollow embeddings are more recent than dense
- [ ] Dense embeddings use raw word counts
- [x] Hollow eddings have most of their coordinates at zero, denses are learned and fully filled
- [ ] There is no background difference, only size

> Explanation:
> - **Creuse** (Spare): large vector with mostly zeros (e.g. TF·IDF on 50,000 words vocabulary).
> - **Dense**: a small, fully-filled vector, learned by a network of neurons (e.g. BERT, Word2Vec).
> The dense embeddings capture the **semantic**, the hollows capture the **presence of terms**.




---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### Why is the evaluation of an IR system indispensable?

- [ ] To reduce index size
- [ ] To increase indexing speed
- [x] To objectively compare different systems and validate their effectiveness
- [ ] To automatically generate queries

> Explanation:
> The rigorous evaluation allows for **comparing IR** systems on reference collections with pre-established judgements of relevance.
> Without evaluation (such as the one introduced by the Cranfield project), it is impossible to know whether one system is better than another.




---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### Among these elements, which are measurements of distance or similarity used in IR? (several possible responses)

- [x] Cosinus distance (Cosine Distance)
- [x] Euclidian distance (Euclidean Distance)
- [ ] Shannon entropy
- [x] Distance from Hamming (Hamming Distance)

> Explanation:
> - **Distance cosinus**: widely used for term vectors (measures the angle between two vectors).
> - **Euclidian distance**: measures the classical geometric distance.
> - **Distance from Hamming**: used for binary vectors.
> - Shannon's**entropy** is a measure of uncertainty in information theory, not a measure of distance between documents.




---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### Why is it said that the query in IR is "soft" (Loose Query)?

- [ ] Because it's always short
- [x] Because the user can express it in natural language without knowing the internal structure of the collection
- [ ] Because it only returns one result
- [ ] Because she always uses a Boolean operator

> Explanation:
> A **loose query** (Loose Query Formalism) means that the user does not need to know the formal language, structure or metadata of the collection.
> Type "meteo Paris tomorrow" in a search engine is a loose query: informal, ambiguous, but understood by the IR system.




---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### What is the difference between "characterizing a document" and "comparing two documents" with distance?

- [ ] There is no difference
- [ ] Characterize compares two documents, compares a single
- [x] Characterize summarizes a single document via its features; compare the similarity between two documents
- [ ] Compare only for visualization

> Explanation:
> - **Characterize a document**: **features** form his individual numerical summary (what he is in himself).
> - **Compare two documents**: **distance** quantifies their relationship (how similar they are).
> - **Characterize a model**: the distribution of distances reveals the overall structure of the corpus.




---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### True or False: The relevance of an IR document is an absolute property, independent of the user.

- [ ] True
- [x] False

> Explanation:
> **Failure.** Relevance is **relating to the information needs of the user** (Information Need).
> The same document can be very relevant to one user and totally irrelevant to another, depending on their context and need.




---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### Practical case — An IR system returns 10 documents of which 7 are relevant. The collection contains a total of 20 relevant documents. What is the precision (Precision) of this system?

- [ ] 20 %
- [ ] 35 %
- [x] 70 %
- [ ] 50 %

> Explanation:
> **Precision** = Relevant returned documents / Returned documents = **7 / 10 = 70%**.
> The **recall** would be 7 / 20 = 35%.
> These two measurements are often in tension: increasing the recall (return more documents) tends to decrease the precision.




---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### Practical case — You have to build a research system in a library of 10 million scientific articles. Which component is INDISPENSABLE so that the search is possible in less than a second?

- [ ] A dense, high-dimensional edding
- [ ] A Language Model
- [x] Un index inversé (Inverted Index)
- [ ] A clustering algorithm

> Explanation:
> The Inverted Index (**Inverted Index) is the data structure that makes it possible to search large-scale in real time.
> It combines with each term the list of documents that contain it, allowing you to instantly find the relevant documents without browsing the entire collection.




---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### A researcher compares two political discourses and observes that they share the words "people", "nation", "country" but diverge on "terrorist/security" vs "jobs/education". Which IR approach best captures this thematic difference?

- [ ] Boolean Search for Common Words
- [ ] Gross count of common words
- [x] Vector model with TF·IDF weight
- [ ] Alphabetical sorting of words

> Explanation:
> The **vectorial model with TF·IDF** (Term Frequency – Inverse Document Frequency) weighs words according to their frequency in the document AND their rarity in the collection.
> Very common words everywhere ("people", "nation") receive low weight; the discriminant words ("terrorist", "jobs") receive a high weight, thus capturing the thematic difference.




---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### Practical case — A system returns documents sorted by cosine distance from query. The closest document has a cosine distance of 0.95. What does this value mean?

- [ ] Both vectors are orthogonal (no similarity)
- [ ] Both vectors are opposite
- [x] Both vectors are very similar (low angle, strong similarity)
- [ ] The distance is invalid because it exceeds 0.5

> Explanation:
> **similarity cosinus** measures the angle cosine between two vectors.
> - Value close to **1** → low angle → documents **very similar**.
> - Value close to **0** → 90° angle → documents **orthogonal** (without relation).
> - Value close to **-1** → documents ** opposite**.
> Thus, a score of 0.95 indicates a **very strong similarity** between the document and the query.




---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### Why does Web 2.0 (social networks) pose specific challenges for the IR compared to Web 1.0 (static pages)?

- [ ] Pages are longer
- [ ] Less data
- [x] Content is generated by users, evolves in real time and includes complex social relationships
- [ ] Search engines cannot index social networks

> Explanation:
> The **Web 2.0** generates **dynamics**, **unstructured**, **ephemers** (tweets, stories...) and integrates **social graphs** (which follows which, like what).
> The IR on Web 2.0 must manage: the freshness of information, social authority (influencers), noise, and a wide variety of formats (short text, images, videos, emojis...).




---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### Scenario analysis — An IR system has a precision (Precision) of 90% but a recall (Recall) of 10%. What's the main problem?

- [ ] The system returns too many irrelevant documents
- [x] The system lacks the vast majority of relevant documents
- [ ] The system is too slow
- [ ] Index is poorly constructed

> Explanation:
> A **recall of 10%** means that the system finds only 10% of the relevant existing documents — in ** only 90%**.
> Despite a high precision (what it returns is correct), the system is ** too restrictive**: it filters too aggressively and misses most of the relevant information.
> The **F-measure** (harmonic average precision + recall) would be very low here, revealing this imbalance.




---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### Among these claims on Neural Embeddings, which one is INCORRECTE?

- [ ] They capture semantic relationships between words (synonyms, context)
- [ ] BERT is an example of dense contextual embedding
- [x] They are still less efficient than TF·IDF for semantic research
- [ ] Word2Vec is an example of embedding words

> Explanation:
> The incorrect claim is that the neuronal eddings would still be less effective** than TF·IDF.
> In reality, neuronal eddings (BERT, Sentence-BERT...) **overtake** generally TF·IDF for semantic research because they capture meaning in context, synonyms and paraphrases — which TF·IDF, based on the exact presence of words, cannot do.

text:
Central problem: Convert textual documents to digital vectors to allow searching.
RSV (Retrieval Status Value) = relevance score \(\text{RSV}(d_j, q) \in \mathbb{R}\) → orders documents by relevance.

title: Representation of information : Embeddings — Revision
text:
Frequency of terms
\[\text{tf}_{ij} = \frac{f_{ij}}{\max_k f_{kj}} \quad \Rightarrow \max_i \text{tf}_{ij} = 1\]
💡 Plus un mot apparaît dans un doc → plus il le représente.

title: Representation of information : Embeddings — Revision
section: Fréquence inverse de document (Inverse Document Frequency)
text:
Fréquence inverse de document (Inverse Document Frequency)
\[\text{idf}_i = \log \frac{N}{n_i}\]

\(n_i\) = nb of docs containing the term \(i\)
Term in all docs → \(\text{idf} \approx 0\) (non discriminant)
Rare term → High \(\text{idf}\) (very discriminant)

title: Representation of information : Embeddings — Revision
text:
TF·IDF weight
\[w_{ij} = \text{tf}_{ij} \cdot \text{idf}_i\]
Matrice terme-document \(W \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times N}\) :

Embedding document : \(d_j = W_{\cdot j} \in \mathbb{R}^M\) (colonne)
Embedding terme : \(t_i = W_{i\cdot}^T \in \mathbb{R}^N\) (ligne transposée)

title: Representation of information : Embeddings — Revision
text:
Géométrie
\[d_j = \sum_i \text{tf}_{ij} \cdot \tau_i \quad \text{avec } \tau_i = \text{idf}_i \cdot e_i\]

\(\text{idf}_i\): scale the \(i\) axis (discriminatory basis)
\(\text{tf}_{ij}\): doc coordination in this database

The structure of the document (order, paragraphs) is lost.

text:
Principe de Robertson (1977)

Classer les documents par probabilité décroissante de pertinence → efficacité optimale.

Objectif : Estimer \(P(R=\text{vrai} \mid d_j, q)\) où \(R\) = variable de Bernoulli de pertinence.

title: Representation of information : Embeddings — Revision
text:
Rapport de cotes bayésien (Odds Ratio)
\[O(R \mid d_j, q) = \frac{P(R \mid d_j, q)}{P(\bar{R} \mid d_j, q)} \propto \frac{P(d_j \mid R, q)}{P(d_j \mid \bar{R}, q)}\]

title: Representation of information : Embeddings — Revision
text:
Logistic regression for RI
\[\log O(R \mid d_j, q) = w^T d_j + w_0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad P(R \mid d_j, q) = \sigma(w^T d_j + w_0)\]

Apprentissage par descente de gradient : \(w_{t+1} = w_t - \eta \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}\)
Features typiques : TF·IDF + longueur du document

title: Representation of information : Embeddings — Revision
text:
BIR — Binary Independence Retrieval
Hypothèses :

Occurrences binaires (présent/absent)
Occurrences indépendantes entre termes

RSV :
\[\text{RSV}(d_j,q) \propto \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}_j \cap \mathcal{I}_q} \left[\log\frac{P(t_i|R,q)}{1-P(t_i|R,q)} + \log\frac{1-P(t_i|\bar{R},q)}{P(t_i|\bar{R},q)}\right]\]
Initialization (without feedback):
\[P(t_i|\bar{R},q) = \frac{n_i}{N} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \log\frac{1-P(t_i|\bar{R},q)}{P(t_i|\bar{R},q)} \approx \log\frac{N}{n_i} = \text{idf}_i\]
⚠️ Connexion clé : À l’initialisation, BIR ↔︎ IDF !

title: Representation of information : Embeddings — Revision
text:

title: Neural Embeddings
text:
The classical techniques of representation in information retrieval (Information Retrieval) are based on statistics properties of terms, regardless of their real meaning.
Three large families preceded neuronal embeddings:

TF·IDF : weighs each term by its frequency in the document and its inverse in the collection. It is a representation purely based on the content (Content-based).
Probabilistic Retrieval: estimates the likelihood that a term is relevant to a given query. It also remains rooted in the frequency of terms.
Latent Semantic Indexation — ISL (Latent Semantic Indexing, LSI): factorizes the term-document matrix to extract linear latent concepts. It’s a projection in a space of small size.

In all these cases, the representation of a term is calculated from its intrinsic properties (frequency, global co-occurrence) without taking into account the local context in which it appears.



The central idea of neuronal embeddings is radically different:

The meaning of a term is determined by the context in which it appears.

This intuition, derived from the distributional linguistics, is summarized by the maxim of J.R. Firth (1957): “You will know a word by the company it keeps.” 
Intuition**: two words that appear systematically in the same contexts (e.g. “fast” and “velocity”) probably share a close meaning. Their vector representation should therefore be similar.

title: Neural Embeddings
text:
General principle
Word2Vec is a family of models that learns vectorial representations of words by exploiting their context of occurrence in a text corpus.
Central idea: terms that frequently co-appear in the same contexts receive close vector representations.

Progressive Intuition
To understand what “use context” means, consider these levels of constraint:

Free choice — “The person is …” → Any word is possible.
Choice forced — “The person is … fast” → the lexical field is restricted.
Guided replacement — “The cat plays with the ball” → ball can be replaced with peluche, but not with nuage.

The more precise the context, the more the choice of the target term is forced. This is exactly what Word2Vec is trying to model.
This framework is closely linked to the automatic processing of natural language (NLP), including morpho-syntactic analysis (part-of-speech tagging) and nominal syntagms (noun phrases).

title: Neural Embeddings
text:
Probabilistic formulation
Or a fixed vocabulary. Two random variables are defined:

\(W_T\): the term target (Target Word)
\(W_C\): a term from context (Context Word)

The objective of embedding is to estimate conditional distribution:
\[\mathbb{P}(W_T \mid W_C)\]
pour tous les termes du vocabulaire.
💡 En d’autres termes : étant donné un mot de contexte, quelle est la probabilité que le mot cible soit \(w\) ?

title: Neural Embeddings
text:
Idée principale
Le modèle CBoW (Sac de Mots Continu) cherche à prédire un terme cible à partir de son contexte local.

Direction : contexte → terme cible

Le principe opérationnel est le suivant :

Définir une fenêtre de contexte (window size) de taille \(m\) autour d’un mot cible.
Créer des paires (contexte, cible) à partir des co-occurrences observées.
Entraîner un modèle pour apprendre \(\mathbb{P}(W_T \mid W_C)\).

title: Neural Embeddings
text:
Exemple détaillé
Considérons la phrase célèbre :

“All work and no play makes Jack a dull boy”

Avec une fenêtre de taille 2 (\(m = 2\)) et le mot cible \(W_T = \text{"play"}\) :

Le contexte gauche (2 mots avant) : “and”, “no”
Le contexte droit (2 mots après) : “makes”, “Jack”

Les paires générées sont :
("play", "and")
("play", "no")
("play", "makes")
("play", "Jack")
Chaque paire \((W_T, W_C)\) constitue un exemple d’apprentissage pour estimer \(\mathbb{P}(W_T \mid W_C)\).
💡 En pratique, on itère sur tous les mots du corpus comme cible potentielle, et on génère toutes les paires correspondantes.

title: Neural Embeddings
text:
Formalisation mathématique

Fonction de perte par terme
Pour un terme cible \(W_T\) donné, la perte (loss) est la log-vraisemblance négative sur tous ses mots de contexte :
\[\mathcal{L}(W_T;\,\theta) = -\sum_{W_C \in \text{context}(W_T)} \log\,\mathbb{P}(W_T \mid W_C)\]


Overall loss on the corpus
Assuming the conditional independence of terms (i.i.d. hypothesis), the overall loss on \(\mathcal{X}\)-size corpus \(N\) is:
\[\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{X};\,\theta) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{W_T \in \mathcal{X}} \mathcal{L}(W_T;\,\theta)\]


Optimisation
L’objectif est de trouver les paramètres optimaux :
\[\theta^* = \arg\min_{\theta}\; \mathcal{L}(\mathcal{X};\,\theta)\]
Optimizer is a Neural Network. The \(\theta\) parameters are the weight** of the network, learned by retropropagation of the gradient.
To make learning tractable on large vocabularies, the Negative Sampling is used: instead of calculating the complete distribution over the entire vocabulary at each step, the correct target is compared to a few random negative examples.

title: Neural Embeddings
text:
Word2Vec Network Architecture (CBoW)
The CBoW network consists of three layers:

Input Layer

One-hot representation of context words \(W_{C_1}, W_{C_2}, \ldots, W_{C_m}\)
Dimension: \(N\) (vocabulary size)



Projection layer / hidden layer (Hidden Layer)

Context word encodings are multiplied by the \(W\) weight matrix (\(N \times C\) dimension, where \(C\) is the dimension of the embedding)
The hidden layer is the sum (or average) of projected context vectors
Resulting vector: \(v_C\) of dimension \(C\)



Output Layer (Output Layer)

The hidden vector is multiplied by a second matrix \(W'\) (dimension \(C \times N\))
A function softmax produces a probability distribution on the vocabulary
The predicted term corresponds to the maximum value

The parameters learned are \(\theta = [W, W']\). The probability is approximated by:
\[\mathbb{P}(W_T \mid W_C) \;\sim\; v_T^{\prime\,\top}\, v_C\]
où \(v_C\) est l’encodage du contexte via \(W\), et \(v_T'\) est la colonne correspondant à \(W_T\) dans \(W'\).

title: Neural Embeddings
text:
La fonction Softmax

Définition
La fonction softmax transforme un vecteur de scores réels en distribution de probabilité :
\[\mathbb{P}(W_T \mid W_C) = \frac{\exp\!\left(v_T^{\prime\,\top}\, v_C\right)}{\displaystyle\sum_{v_i} \exp\!\left(v_i^{\prime\,\top}\, v_C\right)}\]


Interpretation

** Numerator**: exponentially amplifies high scores → selecting the most likely term.
Denominator: normalizes the entire vocabulary → ensures that the sum of probabilities is 1.

Softmax is the category generalization of the binary (sigmoid) logistics function. It applies here to a classification problem at \(N\) classes (one per word of vocabulary).
Connecting with the cross-entropy loss (cross-entropy loss): minimizing \(-\log\,\mathbb{P}(W_T \mid W_C)\) reduces the cross-entropy between the predicted distribution and the target distribution (one-hot).

title: Neural Embeddings
text:
Hierarchical Softmax

Problem
The calculation of the denominator of the softmax requires a sum on all vocabulary, namely \(O(N)\) operations at each learning stage. For a vocabulary of 100,000 words, this is prohibitive.


Solution: hierarchical tree
The terms of the vocabulary present hierarchical dependencies (as illustrated for example in WordNet, lexical basis of English). Words can be arranged in a binary tree reflecting this structure.

Each word is a sheet of the tree.
The probability \(\mathbb{P}(W_T \mid W_C)\) is calculated as a product of probability along the root path to the corresponding leaf.

Reduced complexity: \(O(\log N)\) instead of \(O(N)\) to access the probability of a term.
This trick makes the training of Word2Vec practically feasible on very large corpus.

title: Neural Embeddings
text:
Principle: Inversion of prediction
The Skip-gram model is the dual from CBoW. It reverses the direction of prediction:



Model
Directorate
Objective




CBoW
Context → Target
\(\mathbb{P}(W_T \mid W_C)\)


Skip-gram
Target → Background
\(\mathbb{P}(W_C \mid W_T)\)




Idea: Given a target word \(W_T\), predict the words of its context.

title: Neural Embeddings
text:
Architecture Skip-gram
The Skip-gram network is structured as follows:

Enter: one-hot encoding of the Target word \(W_T\) (PhMATH1PH dimension vector)
Projection layer: multiplication by the \(W\) matrix → hidden \(C\) vector
Released: For each position in the context window, a softmax score is calculated via \(W'\), producing \(m\) probability distributions on the vocabulary (one per context position)

The Skip-gram generates more learning pairs than CBoW (a target word generates \(2m\) examples), making it particularly effective on small body and for ** rare words**.
In practice, the Skip-gram with Negative Sampling (SGNS) is one of the most used variants of Word2Vec.

title: Neural Embeddings
text:
Use of trained models
Once Word2Vec is trained, the weights learned constitute the embeddings of the terms:

Software libraries available (gensim, fastText, etc.) to train its own models.
Pre-trained models: embeddingss learned about very large corpus (Google News, Wikipedia) are publicly available.


Application to documentary search
To represent a document in the space of embedding:

The vector of each term of the document is recovered via the correlation table (lookup table).
The average vector of the terms: \(\vec{d} = \frac{1}{|d|} \sum_{w \in d} \vec{v}_w\) is calculated



Similarity measurement
The similarity between documents (or between query and document) is calculated from the Euclidean distance** in the space of embedding.
It is crucial that the similarity measure be consistent with the construction of the embedding. Inadequate action would result in inconsistent results.

title: Neural Embeddings
text:
Motivation and criticism of Word2Vec
Word2Vec learns to predict local co-occurrences of terms, but ** ignores the overall density** of these co-occurrences in the corpus.
Two words that co-appear twice are treated in the same way as two words that co-appear 2000 times, from the point of view of the structure of learning.

** GloVe idea: Co-occurrences common** should have a greater weight in the construction of the embedding.

title: Neural Embeddings
text:
Probabilistic Intuition
The probability of conditional co-occurrence is defined as:
\[\mathbb{P}_{\text{cooc}}(w_k \mid w_i) \propto \frac{\text{card}\{(w_k, w_i)\}}{\text{card}\{(w_i)\}}\]
où \(\text{card}\{(w_k, w_i)\}\) est le nombre de fois où \(w_k\) et \(w_i\) co-apparaissent dans une même fenêtre.

Exemple illustratif
Prenons \(w_1 = \text{"Poisson"}\) et \(w_2 = \text{"Vache"}\) :

💡 Le ratio des probabilités de co-occurrence discrimine mieux que les probabilités brutes. C’est ce ratio que GloVe cherche à capturer dans l’espace vectoriel.

title: Neural Embeddings
text:
Le modèle GloVe

Construction formelle
On définit une fonction paramétrée \(\phi_\theta\) telle que :
\[\phi_\theta(w_i, w_k) = \exp(v_i^\top v_k) = \mathbb{P}_{\text{cooc}}(w_k \mid w_i)\]
By switching to logarithm:
\[v_i^\top v_k = \log\,\mathbb{P}_{\text{cooc}}(w_k \mid w_i) = \log\,\text{card}\{(w_k, w_i)\} - \log\,\text{card}\{(w_i)\}\]
Le terme \(\log\,\text{card}\{(w_i)\}\) ne dépend pas de \(w_k\) : il joue le rôle d’un biais \(b_i\).


Propriété remarquable : mesure de différence
Pour deux termes \(w_i\) et \(w_j\), on peut mesurer leur “différence” vectorielle :
\[\phi_\theta(v_i - v_j,\; w_k) = \frac{\exp(v_i^\top v_k)}{\exp(v_j^\top v_k)} = \frac{\mathbb{P}_{\text{cooc}}(w_k \mid w_i)}{\mathbb{P}_{\text{cooc}}(w_k \mid w_j)}\]
The difference of the embedding vectors encodes the ratio of co-occurrence — which allows vector analogies of the type: *“roy” - “man” + “woman”

title: Neural Embeddings
text:
Glove Loss Function

Objective
Keep the \(v_i^\top v_k\) scalar product as close as possible to logarithm of the number of co-occurrences.


Formula
\[\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{X};\,\theta) = \sum_{w_i, w_k \in \mathcal{X}} \underbrace{\psi\!\left(\text{card}\{(w_k, w_i)\}\right)}_{\text{fenêtre de pondération}} \left(\underbrace{v_i^\top v_k}_{\text{plongement}} + b_i + b_k - \log\,\text{card}\{(w_k, w_i)\}\right)^2\]


La fonction de pondération \(\psi\)
La fonction \(\psi\) contrôle l’importance accordée aux différentes paires selon leur fréquence de co-occurrence :
\[\psi(x) = \begin{cases} \left(\dfrac{x}{x_{\max}}\right)^\alpha & \text{si } x < x_{\max} \\ 1 & \text{sinon} \end{cases}\]
with the conditions at the edges:

\(\psi(0) = 0\): null co-occurrences do not contribute.
\(\psi(\infty) = 1\): Very strong co-occurrences have a maximum unit weight.

\(x_{\max}\) is a threshold above which the weighting is capped. This prevents very frequent co-occurrences (often due to uninformed grammatical words) from dominate learning.
In practice, \(\alpha = 3/4\) and \(x_{\max} = 100\) are commonly used values (Pennington et al. 2014).

title: Neural Embeddings
text:
Properties of embeddings GloVe
2D visualizations (after reducing dimensionality) show coherent geometric structures:

Gender relations: the vectors “roy” → “roy”, “homme” → “femme” are approximately parallel.
Business-leading relations : IBM → Rometty, Exxon → Tillerson, etc. form parallel structures.
Postcodes and cities: the model captures geographical correspondence.
Compare levels: “slow” → “slower” → “slowest” align regularly.

To be remembered: GloVe encodes the semantic and syntactic relations in the form of regular geometrical transformations in vector space.

section: Why do neural models capture nonlinear relationships?
text:
Why do neural models capture nonlinear relationships?
The TF·IDF and LSI models are linear transformations of data (weighting, matrix factorization). They capture correlations.
Word2Vec and GloVe use neural networks with nonlinearities (softmax, exponential) in their learning process. They can therefore encode complex relations between terms that are not reducible to a simple correlation.
For example, the semantic relationship “capitale de” (Paris: France :: Berlin: Germany) is encoded as a regular vector translation — impossible to capture with LSI.

title: Neural Embeddings
text:
From training to application

Training

Software libraries allow you to train your own models on a specialized corpus (medical, legal, etc.).
Drive requires large corpus and significant computing power.



Pre-trained Models

Pre-entry vectors on massive corpus (Wikipedia, Common Crawl) are publicly available.
They are used directly as **lookup table: a word vector of the vocabulary.



Representation of documents
To use embeddings in information retrieval:

Each term of the document is replaced by its embedding vector.
The document is represented by the average of these vectors.
The similarity between query and document is calculated in this vector space.

It is essential that the similarity measure used is coherent with the metric induced by the embedding model. For Word2Vec and GloVe, this is the Euclidian distance (or cosine in some variants).

title: Neural Embeddings
text:
Societal Biais (Societal Biases)
The embeddingss are taught about real texts, which reflect the cultural and social issues present in society.
Studies have shown (Bolukbasi et al., 2016) that problematic analogies naturally emerge:

“Man is computer programmer what woman is to housewife” 

These unwanted associations are inherited from the biased co-occurrences in the training corpus.
debiasing techniques were proposed to correct these associations, but the problem remains open.

title: Neural Embeddings
text:
Technical limitations

External vocabulary (Out-of-Vocabulary, OOV): words not seen in training have no vector. FastText [Bojanowski et al., 2016] partially solves this problem by working at the level of subwords (subwords).
Unresolved polysemia: the same word with several meanings (e.g. “bank”: financial institution vs. river bank) receives a only medium vector. Contextual models like BERT [Devlin et al., 2018] solve this problem.

title: Neural Embeddings
text:
Extensions of Word2Vec and GloVe
Static embeddingss (one vector per word) paved the way for more powerful architectures:

FastText: enriches vectors with information on sub-words (prefixes, suffixes), which improves the management of rare words and morphologically rich languages.
BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers): generates embeddings contextual — the vector of a word changes according to the sentence in which it appears.
** Machine Translation Models** (Machine Translation): use Transformer architectures (Vaswani et al., 2017) for sequential embeddingss.

The border between the information retrieval (IR) and the modern NLP is increasingly blurred. Current dense semantic research techniques (Dense Retrieval) rely directly on BERT and its variants.

title: Neural Embeddings
section: Modern IR: search for nearest neighbour
text:
Modern IR: search for nearest neighbour

Recent information retrieval techniques represent queries and documents through dense vectors, and research becomes a problem of nearer approximate neighbour (Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search).

This evolution illustrates how neuronal embeddings have profoundly transformed discipline.

title: Neural Embeddings
text:
Question 1: Non-linear relations
Why can Word2Vec and GloVe capture nonlinear relationships between terms? 
Nonlinearity comes from the use of exponential functions (softmax, exp) in the learning process. Unlike LSI, which performs linear matrix factorization, Word2Vec optimizes likelihood via a network of neurons with softmax activation, and GloVe minimizes quadratic loss on co-occurrence logarithms. These formulations enable complex geometric relationships (translations, rotations) to be encoded that cannot be linearly represented.

title: Neural Embeddings
text:
Question 2: Basic differences
What are the fundamental differences in the construction of these models? 
CBoW and Skip-gram learn by optimising a local prediction (context, target) in a stochastic way. GloVe, on the other hand, minimizes an overall loss on the whole ** co-occurrence matrix**, weighted by \(\psi\). GloVe therefore explicitly incorporates the global frequency information of co-occurrences, while Word2Vec implicitly processes it.

title: Neural Embeddings
text:
Question 3: Use of embedding
How is the resulting embedding used? 
The weights of the \(W\) matrix (or \(W'\)) are used as the matching table. To represent a document, the average vectors of its terms are calculated. The search is then performed by calculating the Euclidian distance between the query vector and the document vectors.

title: Neural Embeddings
text:
Question 4: Dimensionality
What is the dimensionality involved? 

Vocabulary: \(N\) words (typically \(10^4\) to \(10^6\))
embedding dimension: \(C\) (typically 100 to 300)
\(W\) matrix is \(N \times C\) dimension
\(W'\) matrix is \(C \times N\) dimension
The product \(v_T^{\prime\,\top} v_C\) is a scalar

title: Neural Embeddings
text:
Question 5: Risk of inappropriate relationships
What is the risk of recording inappropriate relationships between terms? 
Co-occurrence reflects the biases present in the training corpus (gender bias, cultural bias, stereotypes). Undesirable associations can be learned and propagated in applications, with potentially important ethical consequences.

title: Representation of Information: Embeddings
text:
Text documents naturally appear as sequences of words. For a computer to process, compare and classify them, it is necessary to convert them into a manipulable digital form: a vector, a distribution, or more generally a embedding.
A embedding is a function that associates to each document (or term) a mathematical representation in a feature space.
Fundamental intuition: moving from a stack of textual documents to a matrix of numbers, while preserving information relevant to research.



Before representing the documents, define a vocabulary (Vocabulary):

Documents are composed of terms (Terms) — typically words separated by spaces.
A vocabulary of \(M\) terms ** relevant** is built from the collection.
This vocabulary serves as a common repository for all documents and queriess.

The choice of vocabulary is crucial: to include too frequent terms (“the”, “de” …) pollutes representation, while too small a vocabulary loses information.



A system of Information Retrieval (Information Retrieval, IR) operates in two main phases:
** Offline phase (Offline):**

The documents are collected.
features are extracted (embedding stage).
A index is built from these features to allow a quick search.

Interactive phase:

The user formulates a query (Query).
The query is processed and projected in the same space as the documents.
The Search Engine calculates the relevance of each document and produces an ordered list (Ranked List).
The user can provide a Relevance Return (Relevance Feedback) to refine the results.

title: Representation of Information: Embeddings
text:
General rating
The following rating is used throughout the course:

\(N\): Number of documents in the collection.
\(d_j \in \mathbb{R}^{[\![N]\!]}\): representation of \(j\)-th document. The space (and its size) depends on the model chosen.
\(M\): vocabulary size.
\(t_i \in \mathbb{R}^{[\![M]\!]}\): representation of \(i\)-th term.
\(\mathcal{I}_j \subseteq [\![M]\!]\): set of \(i\) indices of the terms contained in \(j\).

title: Representation of Information: Embeddings
text:
query and recovery status value

\(q\): representation of query in the same space as documents (depending on the model).
The \(q\) index is used for elements related to query (e.g. \(w_{iq}\)).

To be retained: The central challenge of the RI is to define a function RSV (Retrieval Status Value):
\[\text{RSV}(d_j, q) \in \mathbb{R}\]
qui mesure la pertinence du document \(d_j\) par rapport à la requête \(q\). L’ordonnancement des documents selon leur RSV produit la liste de résultats.

title: Representation of Information: Embeddings
text:
Principe
Le modèle booléen est le modèle de représentation le plus simple. Il repose sur l’idée d’un encodage binaire (Binary Embedding / 1-hot encoding) de chaque terme du vocabulaire.
Représentation d’un terme :
Le \(i\)-ième terme est représenté par un vecteur \(M\)-dimensionnel :
\[t_i = [\delta_{ik}]_{k=1}^{M}\]
where \(\delta_{ik} = 1\) if \(k = i\), \(0\) otherwise. It is a vector with a single \(1\) in the \(i\) position.
Representation of a document:
A \(d_j\) document is represented by the logical OR of the representations of all the terms it contains:
\[d_j = \bigvee_{i \in \mathcal{I}_j} t_i\]
⚠️ Les termes et les documents se trouvent ainsi sur les sommets d’un hypercube \([0,1]^M\). Chaque coordonnée vaut \(0\) ou \(1\).

title: Representation of Information: Embeddings
text:
Requêtes booléennes
Une requête \(q\) est exprimée comme une expression logique générique utilisant les opérateurs AND (\(\wedge\)), OR (\(\vee\)) et NOT (\(\neg\)).
Pour l’évaluation, la requête est convertie en forme normale disjonctive (Disjunctive Normal Form, DNF), c’est-à-dire une disjonction de composantes conjonctives.
La valeur RSV est binaire :
\[\text{RSV}(d_j, q) = \bigvee_k (d_j \stackrel{?}{=} q_k)\]
A correspond (\(\text{RSV} = 1\)) or does not correspond (\(\text{RSV} = 0\)) to the query.

title: Representation of Information: Embeddings
text:
Example with 3 terms
With \(M = 3\) terms: A (\(t_1 = 100\)), B (\(t_2 = 010\)), C (\(t_3 = 001\)).
Either query \(q = A \wedge (B \vee \neg C)\).
Conversion to DNF:
\[q = (A \wedge B \wedge C) \vee (A \wedge B \wedge \neg C) \vee (A \wedge \neg B \wedge \neg C)\]
\[q = \underbrace{111}_{q_1} \vee \underbrace{110}_{q_2} \vee \underbrace{100}_{q_3}\]
Related documents:
Any document of the form \(111\), \(110\) or \(100\) satisfies the query.

AAA (→ \(100\)), AAB (→ \(110\)), ABCC (→ \(111\)), ABCC (→ \(110\)), A (→ \(100\))
CCC (→ \(001\)), BCCC (→ \(011\)), BBBB (→ \(010\))

Venn diagram visualization is very useful: the coloured regions correspond to the cube areas that satisfy the query.

title: Representation of Information: Embeddings
text:
Concrete example
Query: \(q = (\text{Geneva} \wedge \text{particle}) \vee \text{CERN}\)

« Particle physics is well-studented in Geneva » → contains Geneva ET particle
“CERN leads the search for W boson” → contains CERN
« EU investments in searching for new items » → contains particle but not Geneva or CERN
“Geneva is a place for scientific research” → contains Geneva but not particle or CERN
“The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog” → no relevant terms

title: Representation of Information: Embeddings
text:
Benefits and limitations
Pros benefits:

Simple and formal model.
Explicit and strict Query (similar to SQL).
Easy to implement.

Limitations (Cons):

Some queries are difficult to express in Boolean logic.
binary correspondence → sensitive to exact formulation.
No scheduling among relevant documents or non-relevant documents.
Can return too little or too many documents.
Probably unscalable.

Identified needs:

A more flexible formalism of query → Query-by-Example (QbE)
A continuum of relevance → \(\text{RSV}(d_j, q) \in [0, 1]\)

title: Representation of Information: Embeddings
text:
General principle
The Sac de Mots (Bag of Words, BoW) model is a representation in which:

Terms are the units constituting the vocabulary (e.g. words separated by spaces).
The terms are considered to be independent and unordered entities.
The terms appear with multiplicities (frequencies) → we speak of “bag” (bag) rather than overall (set).

The structure of the document (paragraphs, title, word order…) is lost. Only the frequencies of appearance of the terms are kept.
Although presented here for the text, the BoW model applies to other media (images, audio): the terms then become generic “patterns”.

title: Representation of Information: Embeddings
text:
Frequency of terms (Term Frequency, TF)

Definition
Rather than simply noting the presence or absence of a term (binary encoding), its ** occurrences** are counted.
** Founder’s hyposthesis:** The more frequently a word appears in a document, the more representative that word is of the document.
It defines:

\(f_{ij}\): gross number of occurrences of the term \(i\) in \(j\).
\(\text{tf}_{ij}\): Standardized frequency of the term \(i\) in \(j\):

\[\text{tf}_{ij} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=} \frac{f_{ij}}{\max_k f_{kj}}\]
La normalisation par le terme le plus fréquent garantit \(\max_i \text{tf}_{ij} = 1\).
💡 Cette normalisation permet de comparer des documents de longueurs différentes sur un pied d’égalité.

title: Representation of Information: Embeddings
section: Fréquence Inverse de Document (Inverse Document Frequency, IDF)
text:
Fréquence Inverse de Document (Inverse Document Frequency, IDF)

Définition
La TF seule ne suffit pas : un terme très fréquent dans tous les documents (ex. « le », « est »…) n’est pas discriminant.
On introduit l’IDF pour mesurer le pouvoir discriminant du terme \(i\) dans la collection :
\[\text{idf}_i \stackrel{\text{def}}{=} \log \left(\frac{n_i}{N}\right)^{-1} = \log \frac{N}{n_i}\]
where \(n_i\) is the number of documents containing the term \(i\).


Interpretation

If a term is present in all documents (\(n_i \approx N\)) → \(\text{idf}_i \approx 0\) → non-discriminatory.
If a term is present in very few documents (\(n_i \ll N\)) → \(\text{idf}_i\) is great → very discriminating.

The IDF penalizes ubiquitous terms and values rare and specific terms.

title: Representation of Information: Embeddings
text:
Weighting scheme TF·IDF

Definition of weight
The weight of the term \(i\) in \(j\) is:
\[w_{ij} = \text{tf}_{ij} \cdot \text{idf}_i\]
C’est le schéma de pondération TF·IDF, et il constitue un embedding de documents et de termes.


La matrice terme-document
L’ensemble des poids forme la matrice terme-document \(W \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times N}\) :
\[W = \begin{pmatrix} w_{11} & \cdots & w_{1N} \\ \vdots & w_{ij} & \vdots \\ w_{M1} & \cdots & w_{MN} \end{pmatrix}\]


Embedded documents
\(j\) is represented by the column vector of \(W\):
\[d_j = W_{\cdot j} = [w_{1j}, \ldots, w_{ij}, \ldots, w_{Mj}]^T \in \mathbb{R}^M\]


Embedding des termes
Le terme \(i\) est représenté par le vecteur ligne de \(W\) (transposé) :
\[t_i = (W_{i\cdot})^T = [w_{i1}, \ldots, w_{ij}, \ldots, w_{iN}]^T \in \mathbb{R}^N\]
The term is thus represented by its presence in the collection: two similar terms will have similar vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^N\).

title: Representation of Information: Embeddings
text:
Example: Tag Cloud (Tag Cloud)
A **Tag Cloud is a direct view of the TF·IDF:

The size of each word is proportional to its weight \(w_{ij} = \text{tf}_{ij} \cdot \text{idf}_i\).
Very common words in a document and rare in the collection appear in large.
The ubiquitous words in the collection (e.g. “photo”) appear in small numbers despite their frequency.

title: Representation of Information: Embeddings
text:
Geometry of TF·IDF embedding

Vector interpretation
The \(j\) document can be seen as a linear combination in \(\mathbb{R}^M\):
\[d_j = \sum_i w_{ij} e_i = \sum_i (\text{tf}_{ij} \cdot \text{idf}_i) e_i = \sum_i \text{tf}_{ij} \tau_i\]
où \(\tau_i = \text{idf}_i \cdot e_i\) est la base discriminante associée au terme \(i\).


Rôle de chaque facteur

\(\text{idf}_i\) (commun à tous les documents) : scale la dimension \(i\) selon le pouvoir discriminant du terme. Il transforme la base canonique \(\{e_i\}\) en une base pondérée \(\{\tau_i\}\).
\(\text{tf}_{ij}\) : constitue la vraie coordonnée du document \(j\) dans cette base discriminante.

💡 Géométriquement, l’IDF étire ou contracte les axes de l’espace selon l’importance des termes. Les coordonnées dans cet espace étiré sont les fréquences TF.

title: Representation of Information: Embeddings
text:
Vue d’ensemble
Les embeddings TF·IDF servent de fondation pour plusieurs modèles de récupération classiques :

Modèle vectoriel (Vector Space Retrieval) : similarité géométrique par cosinus.
Récupération par indépendance binaire (Binary Independence Retrieval, BIR) : estimation probabiliste de la pertinence → conduit au modèle BM25.

Ces modèles s’appliquent au texte mais aussi aux médias (images, audio) via des embeddings adaptés.

title: Representation of Information: Embeddings
text:
Principe
Avec le schéma TF·IDF, chaque document \(d_j\) est un vecteur de \(\mathbb{R}^M\).
On peut donc utiliser l’algèbre de cet espace vectoriel pour mesurer la similarité entre documents et requêtes.
Paradigme Query-by-Example (QbE) :
La requête est traitée comme un document exemple. Elle est projetée dans le même espace \(\mathbb{R}^M\) avec le même embedding TF·IDF :
\[q \in \mathbb{R}^M\]
The RSV is then calculated from the geometric similarity between \(d_j\) and \(q\).

title: Representation of Information: Embeddings
text:
First attempt: Euclidian distance
A first idea would be:
\[\text{RSV}(d_j, q) = \|q - d_j\|\]
Cependant, cette mesure est sensible à la norme des vecteurs (longueur des documents). Un long document contenant les mêmes termes qu’un court document aurait une distance plus grande, ce qui n’est pas souhaitable.

title: Representation of Information: Embeddings
text:
Notion de similarité ensembliste
L’embedding BoW repose sur l’idée de sac de termes : la similarité devrait refléter l’intersection des ensembles de termes.
En notation ensembliste, si \(\hat{d}_j\) est l’ensemble des termes du document \(j\) et \(\hat{q}\) l’ensemble des termes de la requête :
\[\text{RSV}(\hat{d}_j, \hat{q}) = |\hat{d}_j \cap \hat{q}|\]
Algebraic version (in binary space):
\[\text{RSV}(d_j, q) = \sum_i w_{ij} w_{iq} = w_{\cdot j}^T w_{\cdot q} = \langle d_j, q \rangle\]
avec \(w_{ij} = 1\) si le terme \(i\) est dans le document \(j\), \(0\) sinon.

title: Representation of Information: Embeddings
text:
Mesures de similarité
En passant à l’embedding continu (TF·IDF), on obtient plusieurs mesures de similarité par extension de la notion d’intersection :








Mesure
Formule continue
Formule binaire




Matching
\(\langle d_j, q \rangle\)
\(\|\hat{d}_j \cap \hat{q}\|\)


Cosinus
\(\frac{\langle d_j, q \rangle}{\|d_j\| \|q\|}\)
\(\frac{\|\hat{d}_j \cap \hat{q}\|}{|\hat{d}_j|^{1/2} |\hat{q}|^{1/2}}\)


Dice
\(\frac{2\langle d_j, q \rangle}{\sum_i (w_{ij} + w_{iq})}\)
\(\frac{2|\hat{d}_j \cap \hat{q}|}{|\hat{d}_j| + |\hat{q}|}\)


Overlap
\(\frac{\langle d_j, q \rangle}{\min(\sum_i w_{ij}, \sum_i w_{iq})}\)
\(\frac{|\hat{d}_j \cap \hat{q}|}{\min(|\hat{d}_j|, |\hat{q}|)}\)


Jaccard
\(\approx \frac{\langle d_j, q \rangle}{\sum_i \max(w_{ij}, w_{iq})}\)
\(\frac{|\hat{d}_j \cap \hat{q}|}{|\hat{d}_j \cup \hat{q}|}\)

title: Representation of Information: Embeddings
text:
Similarité cosinus (Cosine Similarity)

Définition
La mesure la plus utilisée en pratique est la similarité cosinus :
\[\text{RSV}(d_j, q) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=} \cos(\angle(d_j, q)) = \frac{\langle d_j, q \rangle}{\|d_j\| \|q\|} = \frac{d_j^T q}{\|d_j\| \|q\|} = \frac{\sum_i w_{ij} w_{iq}}{\left(\sum_i w_{ij}^2\right)^{1/2} \left(\sum_i w_{iq}^2\right)^{1/2}}\]


Properties

\(\text{RSV} \in [-1, 1]\) (in practice \([0, 1]\) with positive weights).
\(\text{RSV} = 1\) if \(d_j\) and \(q\) are perfectly aligned (same direction).
\(\text{RSV} = 0\) if \(d_j\) and \(q\) are orthogonal (no common term).

Cosine similarity is invariant to standard: it measures the angle between vectors, regardless of their length. Two identical documents but one twice as long will have a cosine of 1.
To be retained: Cosinus similarity is the reference measure in vector IR, directly derived from the concept of extended embossing intersection to continuous embeddings.

title: Representation of Information: Embeddings
text:
General principle
The probabilistic approach addresses recovery from the perspective of reliability:
For a query \(q\), there is an ideal set of relevant documents in the collection. This set has properties described by index terms.
Central idea: Formulate the recovery problem as the specification of the properties of the \(\mathcal{R}\) set from the available terms.

title: Representation of Information: Embeddings
text:
ranking principle by probability

Statement (Robertson, 1977)

If the response of a reference system to each query is a ranking of the documents in descending order of probability of utility to the user, then the overall efficiency of the system will be best possible based on the available data.

— Stephen E. Robertson, Journal of Documentation, 1977 


Formulation
Task: Estimate the relevance of the documents and present the results by ** Descending order of usefulness**.
Here, utility = likelihood of relevance → estimate:
\[P(R = \text{vrai} \mid d_j, q)\]
où \(R\) est une variable aléatoire de Bernoulli indiquant la pertinence.

title: Representation of Information: Embeddings
text:
Estimation itérative de l’ensemble \(\mathcal{R}\)
Le processus est itératif :

Le système fournit une réponse initiale.
L’utilisateur juge certains documents comme pertinents ou non pertinents.
Ces jugements sont utilisés comme feedback pour adapter la réponse.
Le processus se répète jusqu’à satisfaction de l’utilisateur.

    B -->|User Judgment| C{Satisfaction?}
    C -->|Yes| D[Query Result]
    C -->|No| E[Adapted System Response]
    E --> B
    B --> F[User marks some documents\nrelevant or non-relevant]

title: Representation of Information: Embeddings
text:
Décision Bayésienne

Problème de seuil
Plutôt que de fixer un seuil absolu \(P(R \mid d_j, q) > \tau\), on utilise le rapport de cotes (Odds Ratio) bayésien :
\[O(R \mid d_j, q) = \frac{P(R = \text{vrai} \mid d_j, q)}{P(R = \text{faux} \mid d_j, q)} = \frac{P(R \mid d_j, q)}{P(\bar{R} \mid d_j, q)}\]


Application of Bayes Theorem
\[O(R \mid d_j, q) = \frac{P(d_j \mid R, q) P(R \mid q)}{P(d_j \mid \bar{R}, q) P(\bar{R} \mid q)}\]
Comme \(P(R \mid q)\) est constant pour tous les documents, on obtient :
\[O(R \mid d_j, q) \propto \frac{P(d_j \mid R, q)}{P(d_j \mid \bar{R}, q)}\]

title: Representation of Information: Embeddings
text:
Logistic regression for RI

Model
If it is assumed that the log-value ratio is a log-linear function of the features of the document:
\[\log O(R \mid d_j, q) = \phi_\theta(d_j, q) = w^T d_j + w_0\]
Alors :
\[P(R \mid d_j, q) = \sigma_\theta(d_j) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(w^T d_j + w_0)}}\]
with \(\theta = [w, w_0]\) the parameters to learn.


Learning
\(\theta\) parameters are learned by Logistic Regression:

Calculate the \(d_j\) features for each \(j\) document, form the \(D\) matrix.
Select queries, form the \(Q\) matrix.
From pairs of relevance example \((D, Q)\), learn \(\theta\) by gradient descent:

\[w_{t+1} = w_t - \eta \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}(D, Q; \theta)\]
Il s’agit d’un modèle de classification entre pertinence (\(R\)) et non-pertinence (\(\bar{R}\)).
💡 Les features typiques incluent les poids TF·IDF combinés à la longueur du document. N’importe quel embedding peut être utilisé.


Avantages et limites
Avantages :

\(\phi_\theta(d_j, q)\) est un modèle de pertinence absolu.
Apprentissage en ligne avec les jugements de feedback.

Limites :

Le choix des features (embedding) est critique.
Lent si l’apprentissage est effectué au moment de la requête.

title: Representation of Information: Embeddings
section: Récupération par Indépendance Binaire (Binary Independence Retrieval, BIR)
text:
Récupération par Indépendance Binaire (Binary Independence Retrieval, BIR)

Modèle
On suppose :

L’occurrence de chaque terme est binaire (présent ou absent).
Les occurrences des termes sont indépendantes dans le document.

Ces deux hypothèses justifient le nom Binary Independence Retrieval.


Décomposition
Sous ces hypothèses :
\[P(d_j \mid R, q) = \prod_{i \in \mathcal{I}_j} P(t_i \mid R, q) \prod_{i \notin \mathcal{I}_j} (1 - P(t_i \mid R, q))\]
Combining with the odds ratio:
\[O(R \mid d_j, q) \propto \prod_{i \in \mathcal{I}_j} \frac{P(t_i \mid R, q)}{P(t_i \mid \bar{R}, q)} \cdot \prod_{i \notin \mathcal{I}_j} \frac{1 - P(t_i \mid R, q)}{1 - P(t_i \mid \bar{R}, q)}\]


Simplification algébrique
En factorisant les termes présents et absents, et en passant au logarithme :
\[\log O(R \mid d_j, q) \propto \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}_j} \left[ \log \frac{P(t_i \mid R, q)}{1 - P(t_i \mid R, q)} + \log \frac{1 - P(t_i \mid \bar{R}, q)}{P(t_i \mid \bar{R}, q)} \right]\]
The terms missing from query** may be **not known since for \(i \notin \mathcal{I}_q\):
\[P(t_i \mid R, q) = P(t_i \mid \bar{R}, q)\]
D’où le RSV final :
\[\text{RSV}(d_j, q) \propto \sum_{i \in [\![M]\!]} w_{ij} w_{iq} \left[ \log \frac{P(t_i \mid R, q)}{1 - P(t_i \mid R, q)} + \log \frac{1 - P(t_i \mid \bar{R}, q)}{P(t_i \mid \bar{R}, q)} \right]\]
with \(w_{ij}\) and \(w_{iq}\) binary indicators of the term \(i\) in document \(j\) and query \(q\).


Estimation of probabilities
In practice, these probabilities are estimated by counting, using a \(S\) set of the first recovered \(r\) documents as pseudo-feedback positive:

\(r_i\): number of these documents containing the term \(i\).
\(n_i\): total number of documents containing the term \(i\).

Initialization (without feedback):
\[P(t_i \mid R, q) = \rho \text{ (constante)} \quad \text{et} \quad P(t_i \mid \bar{R}, q) = \frac{n_i}{N}\]
On remarque que \(\log \frac{1 - P(t_i \mid \bar{R}, q)}{P(t_i \mid \bar{R}, q)} = \log \frac{N - n_i}{n_i} \approx \log \frac{N}{n_i} = \text{idf}_i\).
⚠️ Connexion avec TF·IDF : à l’initialisation, le BIR est lié à l’IDF !
À l’itération (avec feedback) :
\[P(t_i \mid R, q) = \frac{r_i}{r} \quad \text{et} \quad P(t_i \mid \bar{R}, q) = \frac{n_i - r_i}{N - r}\]
The process continues until convergence.

title: Representation of Information: Embeddings
text:
Model RSJ and formula BM25

Robertson-Sparck-Jones (RSJ)
The basic BIR model evolved to the Robertson-Sparck-Jones (RSJ) model with a weighting:
\[w_i^{\text{RSJ}} = \log \frac{(r_i + 0.5)(N - R - n_i + r_i + 0.5)}{(n_i - r_i + 0.5)(R - r_i + 0.5)}\]


BM25 (Best Match 25 / OKAPI)
La formule BM25 (aussi appelée OKAPI BM25) étend le modèle RSJ en incorporant :

La fréquence du terme dans le document (TF).
La longueur du document (normalization par la longueur).

\[w_i^{\text{BM25}}(tf) = \frac{tf'}{k_1 + tf'} w_i^{\text{RSJ}} = \frac{tf}{k_1\left((1-b) + b\frac{dl}{avdl}\right) + tf} w_i^{\text{RSJ}}\]
where:

\(tf\): frequency of the term in the document.
\(dl\): Document length.
\(avdl\): average length of documents.
\(k_1\) (-1.2), \(b\) (-0.75): control parameters.

The formula BM25 completes (with the terms of the query):
\[\sum_{T \in Q} w^{(1)} \frac{(k_1 + 1)tf}{K + tf} \frac{(k_3 + 1)qtf}{k_3 + qtf}\]
où \(qtf\) est la fréquence du terme dans la requête et \(K = k_1\left((1-b) + b\frac{dl}{avdl}\right)\).
🧠 À retenir : BM25 est le modèle de référence en RI probabiliste, encore utilisé aujourd’hui dans des systèmes modernes (Elasticsearch, Lucene…).

title: Representation of Information: Embeddings
text:
Limites du TF·IDF
L’embedding TF·IDF (BoW) présente deux faiblesses fondamentales liées à la nature du langage :

Synonymie (Synonymy)
Si deux termes \(a\) et \(b\) ont le même sens (ex. « voiture » et « automobile »), leur embedding TF·IDF \(t_a\) et \(t_b\) peut être orthogonal, alors qu’ils devraient être similaires.
⚠️ Un document contenant « automobile » ne sera pas retrouvé par une requête sur « voiture » avec le modèle BoW standard.


Polysémie (Polysemy)
Un terme peut avoir plusieurs sens selon le contexte (ex. « table » → meuble ou tableau de données). Un seul vecteur ne peut pas représenter fidèlement ces sens multiples.

title: Representation of Information: Embeddings
text:
Vers un espace de concepts
Idée fondatrice de la LSI : Les termes sont des compositions de concepts latents (Latent Concepts).
Formellement, on cherche une base orthonormale \(\{c_k\}_{k=1}^K\) pour un espace de concepts telle que \(\langle c_k, c_l \rangle = \delta_{kl}\), et chaque terme \(i\) se décompose comme :
\[t_i = \sum_{k=1}^K \alpha_{ki} c_k\]
Two synonym terms will have similar \(\alpha\) coefficients and will be close in the space of concepts.

title: Representation of Information: Embeddings
text:
Recall : Decomposition in Single Values (SVD)

Definition
For any \(W \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times N}\) matrix, there are two \(U \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times M}\) and \(V \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N}\) orthogonal matrices, and a \(\Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times N}\) diagonal matrice such as:
\[W = U \Sigma V^T\]
avec les valeurs singulières \(\sigma_1 \geq \sigma_2 \geq \ldots \geq 0\) sur la diagonale de \(\Sigma\).


SVD tronquée (Truncated SVD)
Pour \(K \leq \min(M, N)\), on conserve uniquement les \(K\) premières valeurs singulières et vecteurs associés :
\[W_K = U_K \Sigma_K V_K^T\]
with \(U_K \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times K}\), \(\Sigma_K \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times K}\), \(V_K \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times K}\).
\(W_K\) is the \(K\) row approximation of \(W\) in the sense of Frobenius:
\[W_K = \arg\min_{\text{rank}(A) = K} \|W - A\|_F^2\]
💡 Comme \(U\) et \(V\) sont orthogonales, leurs colonnes forment des bases orthonormales : \(\langle u_i, u_j \rangle = \delta_{ij}\) et \(\langle v_i, v_j \rangle = \delta_{ij}\).

title: Representation of Information: Embeddings
text:
Application à la LSI

Embedding de termes orthogonaux
On cherche \(\tilde{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times K}\) tel que les termes \(\tilde{t}_i = \tilde{W}_{i\cdot}\) vérifient :
\[\tilde{W} \tilde{W}^T = I_M \quad \text{(termes décorrélés)}\]


Construction via SVD
Applying the truncated SVD to \(W\): \(W_K = U_K \Sigma_K V_K^T\), we have:
\[W_K W_K^T = U_K \Sigma_K^2 U_K^T\]
d’où :
\[\Sigma_K^{-1} U_K^T W_K W_K^T U_K \Sigma_K^{-1} = I_K\]
Embedding LSI documents:
\[\tilde{d}_j = \Sigma_K^{-1} U_K^T d_j\]
Les coordonnées TF·IDF \(d_j\) sont projetées dans l’espace des concepts \(\mathbb{R}^K\) où les termes sont décorrélés.


Visualisation
La décomposition SVD pour la LSI peut être vue ainsi :

\(U_K\) : matrice des vecteurs de termes (Term Vectors) — colonnes = directions des concepts dans l’espace des termes.
\(\Sigma_K\) : matrice des valeurs singulières — importance de chaque concept.
\(V_K^T\) : matrice des vecteurs de documents (Document Vectors) — représentation des documents dans l’espace des concepts.






flowchart LR
    W["W (M×N)\nTF-IDF Matrix"] --> SVD[Truncated DSV]
    SVD --> Uk["U k (M×K)\nTerm Vectors"]
    SVD --> Sk[(K×K)\nSingle Values]
    SVD --> Vkt["V k^T (K×N)\nDocument Vectors"]

title: Representation of Information: Embeddings
section: Traitement des requêtes en espace LSI
text:
Traitement des requêtes en espace LSI
La requête est traitée comme un document (paradigme QbE) :

Représenter la requête \(q\) dans l’espace TF·IDF standard.
Projeter dans l’espace LSI : \(\tilde{q} = \Sigma_K^{-1} U_K^T q\).
Appliquer la similarité cosinus dans l’espace LSI :

\[\text{RSV}(d_j, q) = \frac{\langle \tilde{d}_j, \tilde{q} \rangle}{\|\tilde{d}_j\| \|\tilde{q}\|}\]
In the LSI space, two documents dealing with the same subject with different vocabularies (synonyms) will be close, which was impossible with the standard BoW.

title: Representation of Information: Embeddings
text:
Choice of rank \(K\)
The \(K\) parameter controls the generalization level:

\(K\) too small → loss of information, too coarse concepts.
\(K\) too large → we get closer to the original TF·IDF space with its problems.
Practical choice: observe the decrease of the singular values \(\sigma_k\) and choose \(K\) at the elbow of the curve.

title: Representation of Information: Embeddings
text:
Index Update
The concept space depends on the original collection. What to do when new documents arrive?
Given the initial \(N\) documents with \(W_K = U_K \Sigma_K V_K^T\), we want to add \(n\) new documents represented by \(D\).

Accurate update strategy

Generate \(D\), the basic representation of new data.
Project on existing representation: \(P = U_K^T D\); Remain: \(H = D - U_K P\).
Calculate an orthonormal \(B\) base of \(H\); projection: \(J = B^T H\).
Form the \(Q = \begin{pmatrix} \Sigma_K & P \\ 0 & J \end{pmatrix}\) matrix, calculate its SVD \(Q = U_n \Sigma_n V_n^T\).
Update: \([U_K B] U_n \Sigma_n \begin{pmatrix} V_K & 0 \\ 0 & I \end{pmatrix} = [W_K \; D]\).



Fold-in folding strategy
A simpler approach: using existing representation for new documents without recalculating the concept base.

Generate \(D\), representation of new data.
Project on existing representation: \(\hat{D} = U_K^T D\).
Concatenate: \([W_K \; D] \approx U_K \Sigma_K [V_K \; \hat{D}]^T\).

Fold-in strategy is an approximation: new documents are supposed to express themselves in existing concepts, without enriching the conceptual space.

title: Representation of Information: Embeddings
text:
Summary of models
Key points to remember:

Relevance to query is central to RI.
The documents are projected in a feature space via embeddings.
The embedding boolean (binary) is not flexible enough.
The Bag of Words model is frequency based (TF·IDF).
The distance cosinus is an extension of the ensemblist intersection.
The probabilistic models consider the terms to be relevant.
The LSI aims to decorate the TF·IDF embedding.
The LSI reveals linear latent factors (concepts).
The low-rank models (based on SVD) are common in many areas.
nonlinear equivalents exist (based on neuron networks).

### Put the construction steps of the S base assembly in HITS in the right order.

title: Indexing to Information Retrieval
text:
The information retrieval (Information Retrieval) is fundamentally linked to large volumes of data. When a user formulates a query, the search engine must calculate — or estimate — a relevancy value (RSV, Retrieval Status Value) for each document in the collection relative to this query.
This naive process is costly: it involves going through all the documents at each query, which is unacceptable on a large scale.


The similarity between a document and a query can only be calculated ** at the time of the query** (at query time). However, part of the work can be anticipated during a phase of offline pretreatment (offline preprocessing).
The central idea of indexing is simple: organize data in advance so that it can be accessed more quickly during queries, at the cost of building the index and additional storage space.



The information retrieval system operates in two main phases:
** Offline phase (Offline):**

Extracting characteristics (Feature extraction) from documents
Construction of index (Indexing) from these characteristics

Interactive phase (Online):

Formulation of query by user
Treatment of query (Query processing)
Search through the similarity engine (Search engine)
Ranking of results (Rank by survey)
View and Relevancy Return (Relevance feedback)

Indexing occurs in the offline phase: it prepares a data structure that will allow the online phase to be fast.
