text:
Abstract Data Type
From an algorithmic point of view, an index must support three fundamental operations:

Insertion (insert, add, put): add new data to index
Deletion (remove, delete): remove data from index
Research (search, find, get): find data according to a criterion

title: Indexing to Information Retrieval
text:
The fundamental compromise
The index uses data properties and anticipated access modes to make likely access quick — possibly at the cost of making access unlikely slower — at the cost of increased storage.
We’re talking about a triple compromise:

Time of query (query time): reduced with index
indexing time: construction cost of index
Storage space (space): index occupies additional memory

To be remembered: an index depends both on the properties of the data and of the type of queries expected. Data without structure, or whose access mode is unknown, cannot be indexed effectively.

title: Indexing to Information Retrieval
text:
Indexed search vs. exhaustive search
The exhaustive search (exhaustive search) covers all N items in the collection: its complexity is O(N).
The index search aims to drastically reduce this cost by exploiting the index structure, ideally at O(log N) or better.

title: Indexing to Information Retrieval
text:
The principle of intersection indexation
Recall The RSV formula based on the cosine similarity between a \(d_j\) document and a query \(q\):
\[\text{RSV}(d_j, q) = \frac{\langle d_j, q \rangle}{\|d_j\| \|q\|} = \frac{\sum_i w_{ij} w_{iq}}{(\sum_i w_{ij}^2)^{1/2} (\sum_i w_{iq}^2)^{1/2}}\]
On peut voir cela comme une version continue de l’intersection d’ensembles :
\[\text{RSV}(\hat{d}_j, \hat{q}) = \frac{|\hat{d}_j \cap \hat{q}|}{|\hat{d}_j|^{1/2} |\hat{q}|^{1/2}}\]

title: Indexing to Information Retrieval
text:
Key observation
Basic observation: \(w_{ij} \cdot w_{iq} \neq 0\) if and only if \(w_{ij} \neq 0\) and \(w_{iq} \neq 0\).
In other words, a term contributes to the score of a document ** only if it appears both in the document and in the query**.
However, a query usually contains only a few terms among the thousands or millions possible. Calculating the sum of \(\sum_{i=1}^{M} w_{ij} w_{iq}\) on all M terms is therefore a waste of resources.
It is much more efficient to calculate:
\[\sum_{i \in \mathbb{1}_j \cap \mathbb{1}_q} w_{ij} w_{iq}\]
où \(\mathbb{1}_j\) désigne l’ensemble des termes présents dans le document \(j\) et \(\mathbb{1}_q\) l’ensemble des termes de la requête.

title: Indexing to Information Retrieval
text:
Reformulation du problème
Au lieu de demander “quels termes sont contenus dans le document \(j\) et dans la requête \(q\) ?”, on reformule en : “quels documents contiennent ce terme de la requête ?”
Ce renversement de perspective est le cœur du fichier inversé.

title: Indexing to Information Retrieval
section: Approche naïve vs. approche avec fichier inversé
text:
Approche naïve vs. approche avec fichier inversé
Approche naïve — O(M × N) :
procedure ComputeRSV(W, q):
    Normaliser la requête q
    r = 0
    pour j dans [1..N]:          // O(N) documents
        pour i dans [1..M]:      // O(M) termes
            r[j] = r[j] + w_ij * w_iq
Approche avec fichier inversé — O(|𝕀_q|) :
procedure ComputeRSV(W, q):
    Normaliser la requête q
    r = 0
    pour i dans 𝕀_q:                          // O(|𝕀_q|) termes de la requête
        pour j dans [1..N] tel que i ∈ 𝕀_j:   // i ∈ 𝕀_j ∩ 𝕀_q
            r[j] = r[j] + w_ij * w_iq
💡 La complexité passe de O(M × N) à O(|𝕀_q|), c’est-à-dire proportionnelle au nombre de termes dans la requête — typiquement très petit !

title: Indexing to Information Retrieval
text:
Construction du fichier inversé
Pour que la recherche de “tous les documents contenant le terme \(i\)” soit en O(1), on construit une liste inversée :
\[i \rightarrow \{j \mid i \in \mathbb{1}_j\}\]
Each term points to the list of documents containing it (with their associated weight).
An inverted file consists of two parts:

The dictionary (Dictionary): contains terms (with global information like the IDF)
The posting file (Posting file): contains, for each term, the list of documents with their frequencies

title: Indexing to Information Retrieval
text:
Construction process
The construction of an inverted file follows several steps:

Extraction (Extraction): for each document, list the couples (term, doc id)
Tri (Sorting): sort all these pairs by term and then by doc id
Compacting (Compaction): grouping the occurrences of the same term in the same document
Factorization: separate dictionary (term → total frequency) from postings (doc id, local frequency)
Miscellaneous operations: compression of the posting file, optimizations…

Remember: the inverted file is the ** indexing structure most used in practice** for text search. This is the basis of all modern search engines.

title: Indexing to Information Retrieval
text:
Why the search by similarity?
With the emergence of vector representations (embeddings) learned by models of Machine Learning (minimization of quadratic error — MMSE), the data are organized in a Euclidian space. The match search then corresponds to the search for the next ** neighbour** (Nearest Neighbor Search, NNS).

title: Indexing to Information Retrieval
text:
Neighbourhood queries Types
Two main types of queries:
Queries per radius (Ranges queries, ε-queries):

Find all neighbours in a radius ε > 0 around the query
Result: a variable size set

Queries of nearest k neighbours (k-NN queries):

Find the closest neighbors k to a query
Result: exactly k elements

These two types of queries assume the structure of a metric space \((\Omega, d)\), i.e. a space with a distance verifying symmetry, separation and triangular inequality.

title: Indexing to Information Retrieval
text:
Space index principle
Given a query \(q\), to find its closest neighbours effectively:
** Offline phase:**

Partition the space into cells (buckets) containing part of the data
Capture cell relationships via a structure (tree, graph)

Online phase:

Identify the cell containing query
All data from this cell (and neighbouring cells) are candidate
Exploit cell relationships to expand research if necessary

The fundamental idea is that close data in space are likely to be in the same or neighbouring cells.

title: Indexing to Information Retrieval
text:
Introduction
The k-d-Trees (k-dimensional trees), proposed by Bentley in 1975, are multidimensional binary research trees. Their principle is simple:

Alternate the dimensions and divide the data into two halves recursively.

title: Indexing to Information Retrieval
text:
Construction algorithm
procedure KDTree(T, X, d):
    // T : arbre, X : données ⊂ ℝ^D, d : dimension courante
    tant que X n'est pas vide :
        d ← (d + 1) mod D           // alterner les dimensions
        Trier X selon la dimension d
        x ← médiane(X)              // point de coupure
        Ajouter x dans T comme nœud v
        X.remove(x)
        Diviser X en X_right et X_left par rapport à x
        v.right ← KDTree(T, X_right, d)
        v.left  ← KDTree(T, X_left, d)

title: Indexing to Information Retrieval
text:
Partitioning strategies
There are two main variants:
Data-based partnership (median):

The cut-off point is the median of the data according to the current dimension
Guarantees balanced sub-trees
Cut-off depends on data distribution

Partitioning based on coordinates (average):

The cut-off point is the average of the space according to the current dimension
The cut divides the space into equal regions
Can generate imbalances if data are irregularly distributed

title: Indexing to Information Retrieval
text:
Search algorithm
For a given query \(q\):

** Descend the tree** with \(q\) to locate the cell to which it belongs → 1-NN candidate
Use Euclidean geometry (triangular inequality) to eliminate whole branches of the tree
** Extend to k-NN** by climbing the tree and exploring potentially useful branches

The depth of the tree is O(log b N), which can allow a very efficient search.

title: Indexing to Information Retrieval
text:
Limitations on k-d-Trees
Despite their elegance, k-d-Trees suffer from several important limitations:

Partitioning “guillotine” (guillotine partitioning): straight cuts are not always well adapted to the form of the data
Random dimensions: the rotation of dimensions (line 4 of the algorithm) does not take into account the variability of the data in each dimension → requires heuristics
Médiction de la dimensionality (Curse of dimensionality): in high dimension, k-d-Trees degenerate and their effectiveness collapses

Variants such as Ball-Trees offer more flexibility and better manage some data distributions.

title: Indexing to Information Retrieval
text:
General principle
Pivot indexing uses a set of representative points (pivots) \(\mathcal{P} \subset \mathcal{X}\) as mark points (landmarks) in space.
The idea is that the distances between the data and these pivots allow** to exclude candidates** without calculating all the exact distances.

title: Indexing to Information Retrieval
text:
Algorithm
procedure PivotIndexing(X, q):

    // Phase hors-ligne
    Sélectionner P ⊂ X
    Calculer et stocker f(x, p) pour tout x ∈ X, p ∈ P

    // Phase en ligne
    Calculer f(q, p) pour tout p ∈ P
    Sélectionner les cellules pertinentes
    Toutes les données de ces cellules sont candidates au k-NN
The key question is: how to select the pivots \(\mathcal{P}\) to maximize the effectiveness of exclusion?

title: Indexing to Information Retrieval
text:
The Euclidian exclusion rule
The theoretical basis for pivot indexing is** triangular inequality**:
\[d(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q}) \leq d(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{x}) + d(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{q}) \implies d(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{x}) \geq d(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q}) - d(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{x})\]
\[d(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{x}) \leq d(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q}) + d(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{x}) \implies d(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{x}) \geq d(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{x}) - d(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q})\]
By combining these two inequalities:
\[d(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{x}) \geq \underbrace{|d(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{x})}_{\text{hors-ligne}} - \underbrace{d(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q})|}_{\text{en ligne}}\]
💡 Cette borne inférieure sur \(d(q, x)\) est calculable sans connaître \(d(q, x)\) directement : on utilise \(d(p, x)\) stocké hors-ligne et \(d(p, q)\) calculé en ligne !

title: Indexing to Information Retrieval
text:
Principe d’exclusion
Le mécanisme d’exclusion fonctionne ainsi :

Indexer les données par rapport aux pivots : \(f(x, p) = d(p, x)\) (stocké hors-ligne)
Calculer la distance de la requête aux pivots : \(f(q, p) = d(p, q)\) (calculé en ligne)
Borner inférieurement la distance de chaque donnée à la requête
Exclure les données dont la borne inférieure dépasse la distance au meilleur candidat connu

title: Indexing to Information Retrieval
text:
L’algorithme AESA
L’Approximating and Eliminating Search Algorithm (AESA), proposé par Micó, Oncina et Vidal (1994), pousse le concept de pivots à l’extrême : les pivots sont construits dynamiquement au cours de la recherche via une stratégie de branch-and-bound.
La borne inférieure utilisée est :
\[d(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{x}_i) \geq \max_{\mathbf{p} \in \mathcal{P}} |d(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{x}_i) - d(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q})| \quad \forall \mathbf{x}_i \in \mathcal{X}\]
The algorithm maintains a \(\mathbf{b}\) vector where \(\mathbf{b}[i]\) is the best known lower terminal for \(d(q, x_i)\).

title: Indexing to Information Retrieval
text:
AESA algorithm (simplified)
procedure AESA(X, q):

    // Phase hors-ligne
    Calculer D : matrice des distances pour X   // O(N²) stockage

    // Phase en ligne
    b ← 0 ; A ← X ; x ← random(A) ; A ← A - {x} ; d_min ← ∞
    tant que A n'est pas vide :
        d_current = d(x, q)
        d_min = min(d_min, d_current)
        Mettre à jour x* si d_current < d_min
        b[i] = max(b[i], |D[x_i, x] - d_current|)  pour tout x_i ∈ A
        A ← A - {x_i | b[i] ≥ d_min}               // Élimination (Bound)
        x ← argmin_A b ; A ← A - {x}               // Sélection (Branch)

title: Indexing to Information Retrieval
text:
Properties and boundaries of EASA
Highlights:

AESA is optimal in number of distance calculations: it minimizes the number of exact distances calculated

Critical limitation:


This represents a storage in O(N2), totally impracticable for large collections

L-EASA (Linear AESA) is a variant that reduces the cost of storage at O(N ×

title: Indexing to Information Retrieval
text:
Why the approximation?
Many algorithms effectively resolve the exact search of the nearest neighbour in low dimension. However, in high dimension, the phenomenon of concentration of distance makes these strategies largely ineffective.
The phenomenon of concentration of distances: in high dimension, all distances between a point of query and points in the collection tend to become equal. It becomes impossible to distinguish close neighbours from distant neighbours.
This phenomenon is a manifestation of the malediction of dimensionality (curse of dimensionality).
To overcome this complexity, we turn to the Approximative Search of the Nearest Neighbor Search (Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search, ANNS).

title: Indexing to Information Retrieval
text:
Formal definition of ANNS
Given a \(\mathcal{X} \subset \Omega\) data set in a \((\Omega, d)\) metric space, a query \(q \in \Omega\), and the \(k > 0\) and \(\varepsilon > 0\) parameters:
Either \(d_k\) the (unknown) distance from \(q\) to its nearest neighbour \(k\)-th. ANNS seeks a set of results such as:

All \(x_i\) with \(d(x_i, q) \leq d_k\) are included (real positives)
No \(x_i\) with \(d(x_i, q) > (1 + \varepsilon) d_k\) is included

Therefore, a grey \([d_k, (1+\varepsilon)d_k]\) area is tolerated where points can be included or excluded without warranty. The \(\varepsilon\) parameter controls the precision/speed compromise.
The overall strategy is to define a new metric \(\tilde{d}(.,.)\) contractive: \(\tilde{d}(x_1, x_2) \leq d(x_1, x_2)\), which is less expensive to calculate and preserve approximately the neighbourhood structure.

title: Indexing to Information Retrieval
text:
Principle
Permutation-based Indexing* PBI is an ANNS technique proposed by Chávez, Figueroa and Navarro (2008). The idea is to characterize each data by the order in which it sees the pivots.
Intuition: if two \(x\) and \(y\) dots are close in space, then they should “see” the pivots in a similar order (the same pivots are close to them, in the same order).

title: Indexing to Information Retrieval
text:
Algorithm
procedure PBI(X, q):

    // Phase hors-ligne
    Sélectionner P ⊂ X
    pour tout x_i ∈ X :
        Ordonner P par distances depuis x_i
        x_i est encodé par le vecteur de permutation σ_i

    // Phase en ligne
    Encoder q en σ_q : ordonner P et retenir la permutation
    Utiliser la distance de permutation pour comparer σ_q et σ_i

title: Indexing to Information Retrieval
text:
Spearman Rho’s measurement
To compare two \(\sigma\) and \(\theta\) permutations of \([\![P]\!]\), the measurement of Spearman Rho is used:
\[\rho(\sigma, \theta) = \sum_{i=1}^{P} (\sigma[i] - \theta[i])^2\]
Dans notre contexte, \(\sigma_i[j]\) indique la position du \(j\)-ème pivot dans l’ordre vu depuis \(x_i\). La distance approximative entre la requête et une donnée est alors :
\[\tilde{d}(\mathbf{q}, x_i) = \rho(\sigma_q, \sigma_i) = \sum_{j=1}^{|\mathcal{P}|} (\sigma_q[j] - \sigma_i[j])^2\]

title: Indexing to Information Retrieval
text:
Benefits and acceleration

The calculation of \(\rho\) is fast: it involves only integer comparisons
It can be further accelerated by using reverse files on the pivots:

Set \(N_P\) (number of nearby pivots considered)
Via inverted files, consider only data whose nearest pivot \(N_P\) have a ** common intersection** with those of \(q\)

title: Indexing to Information Retrieval
text:
Fundamental principle of LSH
The Locality-Sensitive Hashing (LSH) is a family of hash methods designed specifically for the approximate search of neighbours. The two key principles are:

Similar points → chopped in the same bucket with high probability
Dissimilar points → collision with low probability

It is the opposite of the classic hash that seeks to minimize collisions! Here, we exploit them.

title: Indexing to Information Retrieval
text:
Formal definition
Given \(p_{\text{high}} > 0\), \(p_{\text{low}} > 0\) and \(\tau_{\text{low}} > 0\) thresholds, \(\tau_{\text{high}} > 0\), a \(h\) hash function is called LSH if:

If \(d(x_i, x_j) \leq \tau_{\text{low}}\) then \(\mathbb{P}(h(x_i) = h(x_j)) > p_{\text{high}}\)
If \(d(x_i, x_j) \geq \tau_{\text{high}}\) then \(\mathbb{P}(h(x_i) = h(x_j)) < p_{\text{low}}\)

In practice, several LSH functions are used in parallel to increase the probability of finding the real neighbors.

title: Indexing to Information Retrieval
text:
Examples of LSH functions

** Quasi-optimal hash** (Near-optimal hashing) — Andoni & Indyk (2008): optimal for high-dimensional Euclidian distance
SimHash (Similarity Hash) — Charikar (2002): based on random projections. A vector is chopped according to the sign of its projection on a Gaussian random vector
MinHash: adapted to Jaccard’s similarity between ensembles

title: Indexing to Information Retrieval
text:
Learning to Hash
Faced with the difficulty of designing LSH functions by hand, an emerging tendency is to** learn these functions** directly from data (Learning to Hash, L2H).
Characteristics:

Mostly used for specific applications (images, cross-modal search)
Typical architecture: a binary autoencoder regulated by a network strengthening local sensitivity
Supervised or unsupervised approach according to context

title: Indexing to Information Retrieval
text:
Hierarchical Navigable Small Worlds (HNSW)
The HNSW index (Hierarchical Navigable Small Worlds), proposed by Malkov and Yashunin (2016), is currently the state of art for the approximate search of the closest neighbour in high dimension.
It is based on the construction of a hierarchical hierarchical navigable graph (hierarchical navigable spanner) on the data.

title: Indexing to Information Retrieval
text:
HNSW algorithm
procedure HNSW(X, q):

    // Phase hors-ligne
    Construire un graphe navigable hiérarchique G sur X :
    répéter :
        Connecter chaque donnée à ses k-NN déjà dans G
    jusqu'à : plus de données à indexer

    // Phase en ligne
    répéter :
        Partir d'un nœud aléatoire v
        répéter :
            Se déplacer vers le voisin de v qui se rapproche le plus de q
        jusqu'à : minimum local
        Ajouter v dans l'ensemble des voisins candidats de q
    jusqu'à : assez de candidats collectés

title: Indexing to Information Retrieval
text:
Properties of the HNSW graph
Horizontal structure: the graph is organized in several layers. The upper layers contain few nodes with long connections (fast large-scale navigation), the lower layers contain all nodes with short connections (local refinement).
Greedy navigation: Online search is a great descent in the graph — you always move to the neighbour that is closest to the query.
This principle is inspired by the small navigable worlds (navigable small worlds) of network theory: any node can be reached from any other node in few steps.

title: Indexing to Information Retrieval
text:
The billionaire scale challenge
With the rise of the Machine Learning and the vectorial representations learned (embeddings), the need for effective search of closest neighbours on a very large scale was established. We are talking about collections of several billion vectors**.
Existing techniques do not move to this scale:

One graph over a billion knots is too expensive to build and operate
Memory structures (RAM) become prohibitive

The solution: use short representations (short representations) by data, such as binary hash (binary hash).

title: Indexing to Information Retrieval
text:
Current solutions
Product Quantization (PQ) — Jegu, Twelve, Schmid (2011):

Decomposes space into subspaces and quantifies each independently
Implemented in the library FIISS from Facebook/Meta
Store billions of vectors with reduced memory footprint

Diskann — Subramanya et al. (2019):

Use indexation per graph stored on disk (disk-based)
Allows accurate search on a single node with data too large for RAM

SPANN — Chen et al. (2021):

Use **Inverted Files*
Optimized for data partially in memory and partly on disk

title: Indexing to Information Retrieval
text:
Definition of the MIPS problem
Maximum Inner Product Search (MIPS) consists of finding, for a query \(q\), the \(x^*\) point that maximizes the scalar product:
\[x^* = \underset{x_i \in \mathcal{X}}{\arg\max} \langle x_i, q \rangle\]

title: Indexing to Information Retrieval
section: Lien avec la recherche de plus proche voisin
text:
Lien avec la recherche de plus proche voisin
En espace euclidien, la distance au carré entre \(x_i\) et \(q\) se décompose comme suit :
\[d(x_i, q)^2 = \langle x_i - q, x_i - q \rangle = \langle x_i, x_i \rangle + \langle q, q \rangle - 2 \langle x_i, q \rangle\]
So:
\[\underset{x_i}{\arg\min} \ d(x_i, q) \quad \text{est lié à} \quad \underset{x_i}{\arg\max} \ \langle x_i, q \rangle\]
⚠️ Ces deux problèmes sont équivalents si et seulement si les vecteurs sont normalisés (de norme 1), car dans ce cas \(\langle x_i, x_i \rangle\) et \(\langle q, q \rangle\) sont des constantes.
💡 MIPS est donc une généralisation de la recherche de plus proche voisin au cas où les vecteurs ne sont pas normalisés. C’est le problème naturel qui émerge dans les systèmes de recommandation et les LLMs (couche d’attention, recherche dans un vocabulaire…).

title: Indexing to Information Retrieval
text:
Solutions
La bibliothèque ScaNN (Scalable Nearest Neighbors) de Google (Guo et al., 2020) propose une solution efficace basée sur une quantification vectorielle anisotrope.

title: Indexing to Information Retrieval
text:
Ce qu’il faut retenir

Les moteurs de recherche ont besoin d’un accès rapide aux données pertinentes (éléments similaires)
L’indexation est une façon de biaiser l’organisation des données pour accélérer certains accès
L’indexation n’a de sens que si l’on peut identifier des structures dans les données ou leur mode d’accès

title: Indexing to Information Retrieval
text:
Les grandes familles d’index
Fichiers Inversés (Inverted Files) :

Très courants pour les requêtes basées sur l’intersection de termes
Fondement de tous les moteurs de recherche textuels modernes

Index spatiaux (Spatial Indexes) :

Créent une hiérarchie de partitions pour exploiter la structure arborescente
Efficaces en faible dimension, mais limités par la malédiction de la dimensionnalité

Encodage binaire (Binary encoding, hachage) :

Une solution de contournement face à la malédiction de la dimensionnalité
Fondement du LSH et des méthodes modernes à grande échelle

🧠 À retenir final : les index sont des structures de données avancées. Ils représentent un compromis entre temps de requête, temps d’indexation et espace de stockage. Le choix d’un index dépend toujours des propriétés des données et des requêtes anticipées.

text:
Text Information Retrieval (information retrieval) is central to the RI domain. Understanding the text means understanding the original support on which all indexing and search models were built.
The basic objectives of this study are:

Understanding the textual information structure for better use
Use text modeling to optimize indexing and search
Understanding ** Text Generation Mechanisms** and Language
Determine whether the same statistical assumptions can apply to any information based on terms

The central idea is that the text is not random: it obeys precise statistical laws that can be used to build effective RI systems.

title: Information Retrieval Textual
section: The benefits of the text for the RI
text:
The benefits of the text for the RI
The text presents several properties particularly favourable to RI, compared to other types of media.

Interpretation benefits

Goodly understood material: the text is a medium controlled for centuries
Readable characteristics: descriptors (root, terms) are directly interpretable by a human
Comparability: it is relatively easy to compare one textual document with itself or another



Computational benefits

Small data: text is compact compared to images or videos
Effective analytical mechanisms: Syntactic analysis (parsing) is well developed
Proven structuring techniques: JSON, XML, and other formats to organize text with precision



Text as a reference model
In spite of its advantages, the text does not escape the traditional challenges of the RI: similarity, indexing, scaling.
The text was the first indexed medium, which generated a very rich scientific literature. It is often used as concept proof for all systems that can be decomposed into “words”, including Bags of Visual Words.

title: Information Retrieval Textual
text:
The Bag of Words Model

Why not use the full TAL?
The Automatic Language Processing (TAL) offers rigorous approaches thanks to advances in language. However:

It is costful in calculation time and resources
It is complex to implement
It is not always necessary: in RI, we work with approximations
It is not always desirable**: we want a flexible formalism that tolerates ambiguity

We are looking for a representation that captures most of the thematic content without needing to reconstruct or generate text.


Definition of the Word Bag Model
The **Bag of Words (BoW) model is based on the following principles:

terms are the constituent units of the document forming the vocabulary (e.g. words separated by spaces)
Terms are considered to be independent and unordered entities
The terms appear with multiplicity (frequency): it is a sac (bag) rather than a set (set)

In this model, the structure is lost (paragraphs, titles, order of words…).


Generalization of the BoW
The BoW model is not limited to text. Since it applies to several media (text, images, audio…), terms must be seen as generic entities: words, visual patterns, acoustic patterns…


BoW model limits

** Grammatical and structural information loss**: the order of words is ignored
Synonymy: two different words can express the same concept
Polysemia: the same word may have several meanings depending on the context

title: Information Retrieval Textual
text:
Overview of the pipeline
Text processing follows a structured pipeline ranging from raw to index terms.





flowchart LR
    A[Document] --> B[Spacing / Formatting]
    B --> C[Tokenization]
    C --> D[Removal of empty words]
    D --> E[Named groups]
    E --> F[Racineisation / Lemmatisation]
    F --> G[Automatic or manual indexing]
    A --> H[Structure recognition]
    H --> G






This pipeline is broken down into three main stages:
Initial treatment:

Tokenization
Delete empty words (stopwords)

** Morphological normalization:**

Rooting (Stemming)
Lemmatisation

Organization of information:

Construction of index
Construction of the thesaurus (vocabulary)

title: Information Retrieval Textual
text:
Tokenization (Tokenization)

Definition
tokenization (also called lexical analysis/lexical analysis, or lexing) is the operation that transforms a raw document (a sequence of bytes) into a sequence of tokens, typically words.
This amounts to defining one or more separators: everything that is not a separator constitutes a token.


Simple cases: French and English
For French and English, natural separators are:

Whitespaces
ponctuation (virgulate, dot, semicolon…)



Complex cases: other languages
The problem of tokenization is much more difficult for other languages:

German: compound words (Komposita) must be decomposed. Example: Suchprogramm = Such + Programm (Research Program)
Arabic and Asian languages: different reading directions, use of special symbols, absence of spaces between words in certain languages (e.g. Chinese, Japanese)



Special cases in tokenization
Tokenization must also manage:

Digital chain: 1990, 90's, 200BC, 17:00, 5pm
Values with units: $5, 5.-SFr, 5.3kg, 1E-16, percentages, ages
Punctuation and acronyms: U.S.A, RTFM (should they be kept as is or broken down?)
markup Tags: JSON, XML (should tags be ignored?)
Shape: cassage (casefolding), dashes, fonts

There is no universal solution: Tokenization choices depend on language, domain and application.

title: Information Retrieval Textual
text:
Removal of Empty Words (Stopword Removal)

Definition
An empty word (stopword) is a non-discriminatory ** word**: it appears in almost all documents and therefore does not provide any useful information to distinguish between documents.
Typical examples in English: “the”, “a”, “of”, “is”, “and”…
These words are grouped into reference files (e.g. stopwords.txt).


Why delete empty words?

They ** occupy space** in the index without bringing value
They do not contribute to the response to queries
In terms of RI: their IDF (Inverse Document Frequency) is very high, making them non-discriminatory

We will see with Zipf’s law that empty words correspond precisely to the very high frequency terms, the deletion of which allows a significant reduction in index size.

title: Information Retrieval Textual
text:
Rooting (Stemming)

Definition
racinization (Stemming) consists in bringing each word back to its root (stem), that is, its truncated form, by removing suffixes.


Porter algorithm
The most famous algorithm is the Porter stemmer (Porter’s steamer), which applies 5 steps of transformation rules on English words.


Possible behaviour
Stemming can be:

Conservative (cautious): does not reduce European to Europe (risk of semantic confusion)
Agressive (earlier): may confuse paste and past, which share the same root but have different meanings



Multilingualism
Stemming algorithms exist for many languages and are available through the NLTK (Natural Language Toolkit) library in Python.


Interest
Rooting ** reduces the redundancy** of vocabulary and improves the quality of text statistics.

title: Information Retrieval Textual
text:
Lemmatization

Definition
lemmatization consists of bringing each word back to its basic form (lemma), taking into account the grammatical context.
Unlike stemming, lemmatization produces linguistically correct forms.


Examples of transformations

Unconjugation : “are”, “is” → “be”
Singularization : “users”, “users”, “user’s” → “user”



Full example
The sentence:

“Users’ wishes are orders”

becomes after lemmatization:

“user wish be order”



Interest
Like stemming, lemmatization** reduces redundancy** and improves statistics. However, it produces more precise results linguistically.

title: Information Retrieval Textual
section: Construction of the Index and Thesaurus
text:
Construction of the Index and Thesaurus

Indexing Vocabulary
The construction of the index vocabulary is based on several choices:

Individual words: each token becomes an index term
Pairs of words or n-grams: consecutive n token sequences
Nominal groups (Noun phrases / groups): combinations Name + Adjective or nominal constructions

Examples of relevant nominal groups:

“Linear algebra”
“Information retrieval” (information retrieval)

These groups form the base of indexation and significantly enrich the precision of the system.

title: Information Retrieval Textual
text:
SOUNDEX

Principle
SOUNDEX is a heuristic class for extending a query to its phonetic equivalents**. The idea is to normalize spelling variants of the same name into a common phonetic representation.

Specific to a language
Mainly used for named ** entities** (own names, surnames)



Example
The name Chebichef can be transliterated in many ways (Chebysheff, Chebyshev, Chebyshev…). SOUNDEX allows them to be grouped under one key.


Algorithm SOUNDEX
The algorithm (used by most SQL languages) works in 5 steps:

Save the first letter. Set all occurrences of: a, e, i, o, u, y, h, w
Replace consonants (including first letter) with their numeric codes
Replace the adjacent identical numbers by one digit, then remove the zeros
If the number of the first saved letter is identical to the first resulting digit, delete this number (keep the letter)
Add zeros if the result contains less than 3 digits. Keep only the first letter and the following 3 digits



Example of application
“Herman” → H655
SOUNDEX thus transforms each token into a form of 4 characters (1 letter + 3 digits), allowing robust phonetic searches.

title: Information Retrieval Textual
text:
Basic issues
The study of the statistical properties of the text seeks to answer key questions:

How is the frequency of terms distributed?
How does the language size (M) grow with the size of the corpus (N)?
How do these factors ** affect the performance** of an IR system?
How to use them for build an adapted IR system?

The ultimate goal is to use the statistical structure of language to optimize the RI.

title: Information Retrieval Textual
text:
Distribution of Terms Frequency

Empirical observations
The analysis of textual corpus reveals a remarkable and universal phenomenon:

Some terms are very common: the 2 most common terms of a text may represent about 10% of all occurrences
Most terms are very rare: about half of the terms of a corpus appear only once (phenomenon of the Hapax Legomena*)



Heavy-tailed distribution
The frequency distribution of the terms is called “heavy-tailed” (heavy-tailed): the vast majority of the probabilistic mass is in the tail of the distribution (the rare terms), not in the head (the frequent terms).
This property has direct implications for index design and weighting models.

title: Information Retrieval Textual
text:
Zipf’s Law

Definition of rank
The rang \(r(i) \in \mathbb{N}\) of a \(i\) term is defined as its position in a list sorted by decreasing frequency.

The most common term is 1
The second most common term has rank 2
And so on…



Zipf Law Statement
Zipf (1949) empirically observed the following relationship:
\[f(i) \propto \frac{1}{r(i)} \quad \text{ou bien} \quad f(i) \cdot r(i) = K \quad (\text{constante})\]
💡 La fréquence d’un terme est inversement proportionnelle à son rang.


Probabilité d’occurrence
Si \(L\) est le nombre total d’occurrences de termes dans le corpus (longueur \(L = \sum_i f(i)\)), alors la probabilité d’occurrence du terme \(i\) est :
\[p(i) = \frac{f(i)}{L} = \frac{K}{r(i)} \quad \text{avec } K \approx 0.1\]
This gives:
\[f(i) = \frac{KL}{r(i)} \quad \text{avec } K \approx 0.1\]
🧠 À retenir : le terme de rang 1 est environ deux fois plus fréquent que celui de rang 2, trois fois plus que celui de rang 3, etc.



Prédiction des fréquences

Calcul du rang
D’après Zipf, un terme \(i\) apparaissant \(f(i) = n\) fois dans un corpus de longueur \(L\) a le rang :
\[r(i) = r_n = \frac{KL}{n}\]
where \(r_n\) is the maximum rank among all terms appearing \(n\) times.


Number of terms of a given frequency
Since \(r_n\) terms appear \(n\) times or more, and \(r_{n+1}\) terms appear \(n+1\) times or more, the \(s_n\) number of terms appearing exactly \(n\) times is:
\[s_n = r_n - r_{n+1} = \frac{KL}{n} - \frac{KL}{n+1} = \frac{KL}{n(n+1)}\]


Fraction de termes hapax
En supposant que le terme de rang le plus élevé apparaît une seule fois, on a \(r_1 = KL\), ce qui donne \(M = r_1 = KL\) (la taille du vocabulaire).
La fraction de termes apparaissant exactement \(n\) fois est :
\[\frac{s_n}{M} = \frac{s_n}{KL} = \frac{1}{n(n+1)}\]
For \(n = 1\) (the hapax legomena), this fraction is:
\[\frac{s_1}{M} = \frac{1}{1 \times 2} = \frac{1}{2}\]
⚠️ Cela confirme empiriquement que la moitié des termes distincts d’un corpus n’apparaissent qu’une seule fois.

💡 Les prédictions de Zipf sont remarquablement proches des valeurs observées, notamment pour les fréquences intermédiaires.




Loi de Zipf comme loi de puissance

Définition
Une loi de la forme \(y = k \cdot x^c\) est appelée loi de puissance (power law).
La loi de Zipf est une loi de puissance avec \(c = -1\) :
\[f(i) = KL \cdot r(i)^{-1} \quad \text{avec } K \approx 0.1\]


Log-log visualization
On a log-log graph, power laws appear as right:
\[\log(f(i)) = \log(KL \cdot r(i)^{-1}) = \log(KL) - \log(r(i))\]
C’est précisément ce qu’on observe sur le corpus Brown, où les données s’alignent quasi-parfaitement sur une droite en échelle log-log, confirmant la loi de Zipf.
⚠️ Des déviations existent aux rangs extrêmes (très fréquents ou très rares), ce qui a motivé la correction de Mandelbrot.




Correction de Mandelbrot (1954)
Pour mieux ajuster les déviations aux extrêmes, Mandelbrot a proposé la généralisation suivante :
\[f(i) = P(r(i) + \rho)^{-B}\]
with empirical parameters:

\(P = 10^{5.4}\)
\(\rho = 100\)
\(B = 1.15\)

This correction significantly improves the adjustment to high rows (infrequent terms), where the pure Zipf law underestimates frequencies.

Theoretical basis
Mandelbrot also proposed a theoretical derivative: the distribution of Zipf-Mandelbrot is that which minimizes the average length of terms for a given entropy (see section on information theory).




Production model and interpretation

Zipf Hypothesis
Zipf speculated that the power law is the result of the Principle of Less Effort:

The** transmitter** (locutor, author) wants a small vocabulary (simple to produce)
The receptor (lister, reader) wants a large vocabulary (less ambiguous to interpret)

The distribution of Zipf would be a ** balance** between these two opposing trends.


Result of Li (1992)
Li showed that the random stroke of letters including spaces generates tokens (sequences of letters) following a zip distribution. This suggests that Zipf’s law could be an artifact of the combinatorial structure of language.


Practical consequences
Zipf’s law has two major implications for the IR:

Advantage: empty words represent a large fraction of the text; removal significantly reduces storage costs and research efforts






Definition of Index Vocabulary by Luhn
Luhn suggested that extreme terms (very common AND very rare) can be eliminated from the index, thus defining two thresholds:

** Upper Cut-Off: eliminates too frequent terms (empty words)
**Lower Cut-Off: eliminates too few terms (hapax, typing errors)

The significant terms (Significant Terms) lie between these two thresholds and correspond to the terms with the highest discriminant value.
This theoretical framework formally justifies the deletion of empty words and extremely rare terms in the construction of the index.

title: Information Retrieval Textual
section: Heap’s Law — Growth of the Vocabulary
text:
Heap’s Law — Growth of the Vocabulary

Issue
How does the size of the vocabulary (number of distinct terms) grow with the size of the corpus?
The size of the vocabulary is not limited to a higher level, especially because of named entities, neologisms and spelling errors.
This law allows us to estimate the growth of the index as the corpus grows.


Statement of Heap’s Law
\[M = k \cdot L^{\beta}\]
où :

\(M\) est la taille du vocabulaire (nombre de termes distincts)
\(L\) est la longueur du corpus (en tokens)
\(k\) et \(\beta\) sont des constantes empiriques



Valeurs empiriques

\(k \approx 10\) à \(100\)
\(\beta \approx 0.4\) à \(0.6\)

💡 Pour \(\beta \approx 0.5\), la taille du vocabulaire croît approximativement comme \(\sqrt{L}\) : si la taille du corpus est multipliée par 4, le vocabulaire est seulement multiplié par 2.


Lien avec la loi de Zipf
La loi de Heap peut être dérivée de la loi de Zipf en supposant que les documents sont générés en échantillonnant des termes selon une distribution zipfienne. Les deux lois sont donc intimement liées.


Implication pratique
La croissance sous-linéaire du vocabulaire indique que l’index n’explose pas proportionnellement à la taille du corpus. Cela est rassurant pour la conception de systèmes de RI à grande échelle.

Entropie du texte

Entropie d’une source de termes
Étant donné un vocabulaire de \(M\) termes, chacun avec une probabilité \(p_i\) d’être échantillonné, le contenu informationnel attendu d’un terme \(T\) est défini par l’entropie de Shannon :
\[I_H(T) = -\sum_{i=1}^{M} p_i \log p_i\]


Maximum ownership
\(I_H(T)\) is maximum when all terms are equiprobable (\(p_i = \frac{1}{M}\)): in this case, \(I_H(T) = \log M\).


Application to the alphabet
For an alphabet of 26 letters:

If letters are equiprobable: \(I_H(T) \approx \log_2(26) \approx 4.7\) bits
Empirical value observed in English: 4.14 bits (letters are not equiprobable)

title: Information Retrieval Textual
text:
Ideal information carrier

Optimization problem
The \(p\) probability distribution of terms that minimizes the average number of letters per term for a fixed \(h\) entropy value is sought.
\[p_r^* = \arg\min_{p_r} \sum_r p_r l_r\]
sous les contraintes :
\[\sum_r p_r = 1, \quad p_r \geq 0\] \[I_H(T) = -\sum_r p_r \log p_r = h\]
où \(l_r\) est la longueur du terme de rang \(r\).


Solution de Mandelbrot
La solution à ce problème d’optimisation est précisément la distribution de Zipf-Mandelbrot :
\[p_r^* = P(r + \rho)^{-B}\]
This constitutes the theoretical foundation of Zipf-Mandelbrot’s law: the empirically observed distribution is that which optimizes the effectiveness of communication.

Legal Associations

Mutual Information
Mutual Information** between two variables \(W_1\) and \(W_2\) measures the statistical dependence between them:
\[I(W_1; W_2) = I_H(W_1) - I_H(W_1 | W_2) = \sum_{w_1, w_2} \mathbb{P}(w_1, w_2) \log \frac{\mathbb{P}(w_1, w_2)}{\mathbb{P}(w_1)\mathbb{P}(w_2)}\]


Interprétation
Si \(W_1\) et \(W_2\) ne co-occurrent jamais (indépendants), alors :
\[\mathbb{P}(W_1, W_2) = \mathbb{P}(w_1)\mathbb{P}(w_2) \quad \Rightarrow \quad I(W_1; W_2) = 0\]
Mutual information is therefore an appropriate measure to study co-occurrence of terms:

Great value of \(I(W_1; W_2)\) → interesting co-occurrence, significant

Text modelling

Text follows approximate generative models that can be used in RI
The Model Bag of Words is the foundation of most textual representations



Zipf Law

Zipf’s law is a typical example of power law emerging from an entity-based generic model
It directly connects the frequency and the range of a term: \(f(i) \cdot r(i) = K\)
It predicts that 50% of the separate terms appear only once
It justifies the deletion of empty words and too few terms



Law of Heap

It allows to estimate the future size of an index



Information Theory

Information Theory provides the tools for modelling information exchange via text

** mutual information** identifies significant co-occurrence between terms

text:
---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### What does the acronym RSV mean in information retrieval (Information Retrieval)?

- [ ] Random Selection Value
- [x] Retrieval Status Value
- [ ] Ranked Scoring Vector
- [ ] Relevance Sampling Value

> Explanation:
> The RSV (Retrieval Status Value) is the relevance score assigned to each document against a query. It is on the basis of this score that documents are ordered from the list of results.




---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### In the Boolean Model, what is the basis for the representation of terms?

- [ ] Frequency of appearance in documents
- [ ] Probability of relevance
- [x] Encodage binaire 1-hot (1-hot encoding)
- [ ] Decomposition in singular values

> Explanation:
> The Boolean model uses a 1-hot encoding: the term $i$ is represented by a $M$-dimensional vector with a $1$ in the $i$ position and $0$ anywhere else. The terms and documents are found on tops of a $[0,1]^M$ hypercube.




---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### What is the possible value of the RSV in the Boolean Model?

- [ ] Any real in $\mathbb{R}$
- [ ] A real in $[0, 1]$
- [x] Only $0$ or $1$
- [ ] A Positive Whole

> Explanation:
> This is the basic limit of the Boolean model: the correspondence is binary — a document corresponds to the query (RSV = 1) or does not match (RSV = 0). There is no sequencing in the relevant documents.




---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### What formula defines the frequency of the standard terms (Term Frequency) $\text{tf}_{ij}$?

- [ ] $\text{tf}_{ij} = f_{ij} \cdot N$
- [ ] $\text{tf}_{ij} = \log(f_{ij} + 1)$
- [x] $\text{tf}_{ij} = \dfrac{f_{ij}}{\max_k f_{kj}}$
- [ ] $\text{tf}_{ij} = \dfrac{f_{ij}}{N}$

> Explanation:
> The standard TF divides the gross frequency of the term $i$ in the $j$ document by the frequency of the most common term in the same document. This guarantees $\max_i \text{tf}_{ij} = 1$ and allows you to compare documents of different lengths.




---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### What does the Inverse Document Frequency measure?

- [ ] Frequency of a term in a document
- [ ] Average length of documents
- [x] The discriminating power of a term in the collection
- [ ] The total number of queries treated

> Explanation:
> The IDF is defined by $\text{idf}_i = \log(N / n_i)$. It measures the discriminant power of the term $i$: if the term appears in all documents ($n_i \approx N$), its IDF is close to $0$ (non-discriminatory). If the term is rare ($n_i \ll N$), its IDF is high.




---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### A term appears in all $N$ documents in the collection. What is the approximate value of its IDF?

- [ ] $\log(N)$
- [ ] $1$
- [x] Close to $0$
- [ ] $N$

> Explanation:
> $\text{idf}_i = \log(N/n_i)$. If $n_i = N$ then $\text{idf}_i = \log(1) = 0$. A term present in all documents is not discriminatory and has a TF·IDF weight zero.




---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### True or False: In the Bag of Words (BoW) template, the order of words in a document is taken into account.

- [ ] True
- [x] False

> Wrong:
> The Bag of Words model treats terms as independent and unordered entities. The structure of the document (order of words, paragraphs, title) is lost. Only the frequency of appearance is kept.




---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### What is the formula of the TF·IDF weight of the term $i$ in the document $j$?

- [ ] $w_{ij} = \text{tf}_{ij} + \text{idf}_i$
- [x] $w_{ij} = \text{tf}_{ij} \cdot \text{idf}_i$
- [ ] $w_{ij} = \dfrac{\text{tf}_{ij}}{\text{idf}_i}$
- [ ] $w_{ij} = \text{tf}_{ij}^{\text{idf}_i}$

> Explanation:
> TF·IDF weight is the product of standard frequency ($\text{tf}_{ij}$) and discriminant power ($\text{idf}_i$). A common term in the document AND rare in the collection will have a high weight.




---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### In the term-document matrix $W \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times N}$, how is the document $j$ represented?

- [ ] By the $j$ line of $W$
- [x] By the $j$ column of $W$, i.e. $d_j = W_{\cdot j} \in \mathbb{R}^M$
- [ ] By the diagonal of $W$
- [ ] By the product $W \cdot W^T$

> Explanation:
> $j$ is represented by the column vector $d_j = W_{\cdot j} = [w_{1j}, \ldots, w_{Mj}]^T \in \mathbb{R}^M$. Symmetrically, the term $i$ is represented by the transposition of the line $i$: $t_i = W_{i\cdot}^T \in \mathbb{R}^N$.




---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### Why is Cosinus similarity preferred at the Euclidian distance in RI?

- [ ] It's faster to calculate
- [ ] It takes into account the position of words
- [x] It is invariant to the standard (length) of vectors
- [ ] It only works with binary values

> Explanation:
> Cosinus similarity measures the angle between two vectors, regardless of their standard. Two identical documents but one twice as long obtain a cosine of 1. Euclidian distance would unfairly penalize longer documents.




---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### What is the cosine similarity formula between $d_j$ and $q$?

- [ ] $\dfrac{\|d_j - q\|}{\|d_j\| + \|q\|}$
- [x] $\dfrac{d_j^T q}{\|d_j\| \|q\|}$
- [ ] $\dfrac{d_j^T q}{\|d_j\| + \|q\|}$
- [ ] $d_j^T q$

> Explanation:
> $\text{RSV}(d_j, q) = \cos(\angle(d_j, q)) = \dfrac{\langle d_j, q \rangle}{\|d_j\| \|q\|} = \dfrac{\sum_i w_{ij} w_{iq}}{(\sum_i w_{ij}^2)^{1/2}(\sum_i w_{iq}^2)^{1/2}}$. It is between $-1$ and $1$ (in practice between $0$ and $1$ with positive weights).




---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### What mathematical notion underlies cosinus similarity in vector model?

- [ ] Distance from Manhattan
- [ ] The standard of Frobenius
- [x] The embodiment intersection extended to continuous embeddings
- [ ] Decomposition into own values

> Explanation:
> In binary representation, $\text{RSV}(\hat{d}_j, \hat{q}) = |\hat{d}_j \cap \hat{q}| = \sum_i w_{ij} w_{iq} = \langle d_j, q \rangle$. Cosinus similarity is a standardized extension of this intersection, allowing the comparison of documents of different lengths.




---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### In the probabilistic model, what is the $R$ variable?

- [ ] The ranking of the document in the list
- [ ] Number of documents found
- [x] A Bernoulli variable indicating whether the document is relevant
- [ ] The reformulated query

> Explanation:
> $R$ is a binary random variable (Bernoulli): $R = \text{vrai}$ if the document is relevant, $R = \text{faux}$ otherwise. The objective is to estimate $P(R = \text{vrai} \mid d_j, q)$ to classify documents by decreasing relevance.




---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### True or False: In the BIR (Binary Independence Retrieval) model, the occurrences of the terms are assumed to be correlated.

- [ ] True
- [x] False

> Wrong:
> The name "Independence" refers precisely to the hypothesis of** independence** of the occurrences of the terms in the documents. This is a simplifying hypothesis rarely verified in practice, but which allows to factor the probability of the document.




---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### What is the link between the IDF and the BIR model at initialization (without feedback)?

- [ ] There is no connection
- [ ] The IDF completely replaces the BIR
- [x] At initialization, the BIR log-odds term is approximately equal to the IDF
- [ ] The IDF is the square root of the BIR score

> Explanation:
> Without feedback, $P(t_i | \bar{R}, q) = n_i/N$, so $\log\frac{1 - P(t_i|\bar{R},q)}{P(t_i|\bar{R},q)} = \log\frac{N - n_i}{n_i} \approx \log\frac{N}{n_i} = \text{idf}_i$. The BIR is thus reduced to an IDF initialisation weighting.




---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### Among the following are the parameters of the formula BM25? (several possible responses)

- [x] $k_1$: TF saturation parameter
- [x] $b$: length normalization parameter
- [ ] $M$: vocabulary size
- [x] $avdl$: average length of documents

> Explanation:
> BM25 introduces $k_1$ ( $M$ is a feature of the collection, not a parameter of BM25.




---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### Why does the model TF·IDF (BoW) fail against synonymy (Synonymy)?

- [ ] Because he doesn't calculate the frequencies correctly
- [ ] Because IDF always sucks for synonyms
- [x] Because two synonym terms have orthogonal vectors in the TF·IDF space
- [ ] Because the W matrix cannot contain synonyms

> Explanation:
> In the TF·IDF space, each term occupies a distinct dimension. Two synonyms (e.g., "car" and "automobile") have orthogonal vectors ($\langle t_i, t_j \rangle = 0$), while they should be close. A document containing "automobile" will not be found by a query on "car".




---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### What is the fundamental property of the $K$ Truncated SVD?

- [ ] It maximizes the trace of the matrix
- [x] It provides the best $K$ row approximation within the meaning of the Frobenius standard
- [ ] It diagonalizes the term-document matrix
- [ ] It minimizes the number of singular nonzero values

> Explanation:
> $W_K = U_K \Sigma_K V_K^T = \arg\min_{\text{rank}(A) = K} \|W - A\|_F^2$. It is the fundamental property of the truncated SVD, which justifies its use for compression and dimension reduction in the LSI.




---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### In the LSI (Latent Semantic Indexing), how is a $d_j$ document projected in the concept space?

- [ ] $\tilde{d}_j = U_K d_j$
- [ ] $\tilde{d}_j = V_K^T d_j$
- [x] $\tilde{d}_j = \Sigma_K^{-1} U_K^T d_j$
- [ ] $\tilde{d}_j = U_K \Sigma_K d_j$

> Explanation:
> The LSI projection is $\tilde{d}_j = \Sigma_K^{-1} U_K^T d_j \in \mathbb{R}^K$. First, $U_K^T$ is applied to project single left vectors into space, then $\Sigma_K^{-1}$ to normalize by the importance of each concept.




---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### An engineer deploys an RI system with a TF·IDF model. Users complain that searching for "car" does not find the documents referring to "automobile". Which technical solution is the most appropriate?

- [ ] Increase the value of $k_1$ in BM25
- [ ] Reduce vocabulary size $M$
- [x] Apply LSI to project into a latent concept space
- [ ] Use a Boolean model with the OR operator

> Explanation:
> The LSI precisely solves the synonymy problem by creating a space of latent concepts where semantically similar terms are found in similar directions. A Boolean model with OR would work for known synonyms, but is not a general and scalable solution.




---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### Practical case — What is the main difference between the exact update strategy (Exact Update) and folding (Fold-in) in the LSI?

- [ ] Fold-in recalculates the entire SVD, the exact non
- [x] The exact enriches the conceptual space, the fold-in projects only into the existing space
- [ ] Both methods are equivalent in quality
- [ ] Fold-in uses $V_K$ while exact uses $U_K$

> Explanation:
> In the fold-in, new documents are projected on the existing basis ($\hat{D} = U_K^T D$) without changing the concept space. This is a quick approximation but the new concepts eventually brought by the new documents are ignored. The exact update partially recalculates SVD to incorporate these new concepts.




---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### In the TF·IDF geometry, what is the exact role of the $\text{idf}_i$ factor on document representation?

- [ ] It normalizes the document vector to standard 1
- [x] It staggers (scale) the $i$ dimension of space, transforming the canonical base $e_i$ into a discriminant base $\tau_i = \text{idf}_i \cdot e_i$
- [ ] It replaces the raw frequency with a logarithmic frequency
- [ ] It projects the document into a space of lower dimension

> Explanation:
> $j$ is written $d_j = \sum_i \text{tf}_{ij} \cdot \tau_i$ with $\tau_i = \text{idf}_i \cdot e_i$. The IDF is common to all documents and transforms the canonical base into a base weighted by the discriminating power of each term. The TF is the real coordinated document in this database.




---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### Among these assertions on the Principle of Ranking by Probability (Probability Ranking Principle, Robertson 1977), which is correct?

- [ ] It recommends that documents be sorted alphabetically
- [ ] It ensures that all relevant documents are found
- [x] It states that classifying documents by decreasing probability of utility gives optimal efficiency
- [ ] It applies only to Boolean models

> Explanation:
> Robertson (1977) states that if the system ranks documents in descending order of probability of utility $P(R \mid d_j, q)$, estimated as accurately as possible, then overall efficiency will be optimal based on available data. This principle underpins the entire probabilistic approach to RI.




---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### True or False: In the LSI, choose $K = M$ (preserving all singular values) solves synonymy problems.

- [ ] True
- [x] False

> Wrong:
> If $K = \min(M, N)$, the truncated SVD becomes the complete SVD and $W_K = W$: we find exactly the original TF·IDF space with all its problems (synonymy, polysemia). The dimension reduction ($K \ll M$) is precisely what forces the model to generalize and group closely related terms.




---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### Practical case — An RI system returns too little or too many documents according to the exact wording of the query. What model is involved and what is its direct alternative?

- [ ] LSI — alternative: BM25
- [x] Boolean model — alternative: vector model with cosinus similarity
- [ ] BM25 — alternative : TF·IDF standard
- [ ] Vector model — alternative: Boolean model

> Explanation:
> This is the classic limit of the Boolean model: a too restrictive query returns nothing, too permissive returns everything, without nuance. The cosinus-similarity vector model produces a continuum of $\in [0,1]$ RSV, allowing an end-of-document ranking regardless of the exact formulation.




---
primaryColor: '#4a90d9'
shuffleQuestions: false
shuffleAnswers: true
locale: en
---

### Among the following proposals, which are advantages of the LSI compared to the standard TF·IDF ? (several possible responses)

- [x] Synonymy Management (Synonymy)
- [x] Decoration of dimensions of the representation space
- [ ] Calculation faster than TF·IDF
- [x] Grouping of semantically close terms in the space of concepts

> Explanation:
> The LSI corrects the two major weaknesses of the TF·IDF: synonymy (different terms, same meaning → close in LSI space) and partial polysemia via decorrelation. On the other hand, it is more costly to calculate (SVD) than the standard TF·IDF.

title: Information Retrieval : Introduction
text:
We live in an era of mass production of digital data (Digital Data Production). The volume of information created, captured, copied and consumed in the world is growing exponentially from year to year.
To give a concrete measure of this reality:

In 2010, the world produced about 2 zettabytes of data.
In 2025, this quantity exceeded 180 zettabytes.

A zettabyte (zetabyte) represents \(2^{70}\) bytes, or 1 billion terabytes. It is so large that it is difficult to intuitively design.
This growth is not linear but exponential: the amount of data doubles every few years, making traditional information management methods insufficient.


Several factors explain this growth:

The democratization of smartphones and connected devices.
The development of social networks (Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, X…).
The digitisation of public and private services (health, education, banking…).
The development of the Internet of Things (IoT).
The generalization of streaming video and audio.

To remember: the amount of digital data available far exceeds the human capacity to process them manually. This is the raison d’être of the Information Retrieval (Information Retrieval).







Photography perfectly illustrates the transition to an entirely digital world.

In 1826, the first photograph was taken: 0 billion photos per year.
In 1930, with the democratization of the silver apparatus, about 1 billion photos are taken each year.
In 2000, at the peak of silver photography (Analog photos), this figure reached 86 billion, before falling sharply with the arrival of digital technology.
In 2011, the total (digital + analog photos) exceeds 380 billion photos per year.

This graph illustrates two important phenomena:

The Technological rupture: Silver photography collapsed in the 2000s, replaced by digital.
The** amplification effect**: by removing the marginal cost of shooting (no need for film), digital multiplies the volume of data produced.

The same logic applies to all forms of content: texts, videos, messages, audio recordings. Digital lowers the cost of production and causes a information avalanche (avalanche information).







The figures illustrating online activity are dizzying. Every minute on the Internet includes:

3.47 million videos watched on YouTube.
625 million videos viewed on TikTok.
3.5 billion Snaps created.
66,000 photos and videos shared on Instagram.
350,000 tweets sent.
231 million e-mails sent.
6.3 million Google searches.
44 million people watching Facebook Live.

These figures highlight the ubiquitous need for research and access to information** in our daily use. Research alone accounts for 21% of the time spent online.
To be remembered: Global connectivity is constantly generating new content and access to information needs. Information Retrieval systems are at the heart of this infrastructure.







The digital world is not stabilizing: it is constantly evolving, and this evolution is accelerating.
A striking example is YouTube:

In 2012: 30 hours of video were uploaded each minute.
In 2024: this figure is 500 hours per minute.

It is a multiplication by 15 in 10 years, illustrating the exponential acceleration of content production.
This poses constant challenges to Information Retrieval systems:

Algorithms must adapt to ever-increasing volumes.
The types of content are diverse (text, image, video, audio, structured data…).
Uses evolve (voice search, multimodal, contextual…).

title: Information Retrieval : Introduction
text:
Motivation: user needs

Understanding user needs

How people spend their time online (2012)
In 2012, studies on Internet use revealed the following distribution of time spent online:

22%: Social Networking
21%: Research (Seaches)
20%: Reading Content
19%: e-mails and communication (Emails/Communication)
13 %: multimedia sites (Multi-media Sites)
5%: Online Shopping

Thus, nearly 41% of online time is devoted to activities directly related to research and information consumption (research + content reading). Information Retrieval is therefore at the heart of digital usage.




Major needs identified

Making informed decisions
Decision Making is a fundamental need of users. Any decision—whether personal, professional or academic—requires access to relevant, reliable and up to date information.
Without structured access to information, decision-making is based on incomplete or biased data.



Manage information avalanche
The information avalanche** (Information Avalanche) is one of the great challenges of our time. Being exposed to a massive volume of information does not mean being better informed: on the contrary, without suitable tools, it generates cognitive overload and disinformation.
It is therefore necessary to implement **Advanced Information Management Processes, capable of:

Filter relevant information.
Organize and structure content.
Present information in an exploitable manner.




Access to large information depots
Access to large information repository is the foundation of Data Science. Machine learning, statistical analysis or data visualisation algorithms are of value only if the underlying data are accessible, represented and comparable.
To be remembered: Information Retrieval is a fundamental building block of Data Science because it makes data exploitable on a large scale.




Bringing structure to raw data
To meet these needs, it is essential to structure raw data (Raw Data). This involves three essential steps:

1. Appropriate Data Representation (Document Representation)
A raw document (text, image, audio, video…) cannot be directly compared or analyzed by an algorithm. One ** formal representation** must be extracted:

For a text: a word frequency vector.
For an image: a color histogram, or a vector of visual characteristics.
For audio: spectral descriptors (MFCC, etc.).

The quality of this representation directly determines the quality of the following analysis.


2. Appropriate Similarity Measurements
Once the documents are represented, you must be able to compare them . Measurements of similarity** (or distance) adapted to the nature of the data are defined for this purpose.

Euclidean distance in a vector space.
Cosine distance for term vectors.
Distance from Hamming for binary data.

The choice of similarity measurement is crucial: a bad measurement leads to inconsistent results, even with good representation.


3. Analysis process: search, learning, visualization
Once represented and comparable, the data can be subjected to analytical processes:

Data mining (Mining): clustering, detection of abnormalities, frequent patterns.
Learning: classification, regression, walking.
Visualization (Visualization): reduction of dimensionality, similarity maps.





The Information Management Pipeline
The general information management process can be summarized as follows:





flowchart LR
    A[Gross documents] --> B[Extraction of characteristics\nFeature Extraction]
    B --> C[Features\nDocument Features]
    C --> D[Appropriate mapping\nAppropriate Mapping]
    D --> E[Representation space\nRepresentation Space]
    E --> F[User Interaction\nUser Interaction]
    F --> G[Decision-making process]
    G --> H[Decision]






This pipeline is universal: it applies to texts, images, videos and any other type of digital data.



Concrete examples

Example 1: Text documents
For a corpus of text documents (Text Documents), the pipeline works as follows:

Extraction of features: The occurrences of each word are counted in each document. We obtain ** terms frequency vectors** (Word Occurrences / Term Frequency vectors).
Appropriate mapping: a transformation (e.g. TF·IDF or dimension reduction) is applied to move from a hollow to a dense representation.
Representation space: documents are projected into a vector space where similar documents are close to each other — visible in the form of a word cloud (Tag Cloud) or thematic map.
User interaction: The user formulates a query, the system returns the most relevant documents.
Decision: The user has access to the information they need.

The notion of word cloud (Tag Cloud / Word Cloud) is a simple but effective visualization of the distribution of terms in a document or corpus.



Example 2: Images
For a collection ofimages (Images), the same pipeline applies:

Extraction of characteristics: color histograms (Color Histograms) are extracted for each image — a compact descriptor representing the colour distribution (red, green, blue).
Appropriate mapping: Histograms are projected into a representation space where visually similar images are close.
Representative space: The images are arranged in a 2D or 3D space according to their visual similarity.
User interaction: the user can navigate in this space, select a reference image, and get the most similar images.
Decision: result in the form of photo collage (Photo Collage) filtered according to the user’s needs.

Color histograms are global ** descriptors**: they capture the colorimetric palette of an image, but ignore the spatial position of the colours. More sophisticated descriptors (SIFT, CNN features) capture more local information.



Example 3: Other types of media
Information Retrieval is not limited to text and images. It applies to:

Audio and video: transcriptions, spectral descriptors, temporal characteristics.
Webpages: hypertext structure, links, metadata.
Messages (e-mail, chat): text content, temporal and social metadata.
Services and processes: log systems, process states.
People, businesses, communities: social graphs, user profiles.
Web 1.0 (static pages), Web 2.0 (social networks), Web 3.0 (Internet of Things / IoT), Web 4.0 (metavers / verse).

To be remembered: any object to which digital characteristics may be associated may be subject to a Information Retrieval. Discipline is therefore universally applicable.

title: Information Retrieval : Introduction
text:
Distance in Information Retrieval

Distance: a central concept

Why is distance fundamental?
The concept of distance (or similarity) is at the heart of Information Retrieval. It answers a simple but fundamental question:

To what extent do two documents deal with the same subject? 

Distance is not only a technical tool: it is the mathematical formalization of the human intuition of resemblance between two contents.



The example of presidential speeches
To illustrate the problem of distance measurement, consider two clouds of words from State of the Union Address:

Speech by George W. Bush (January 29, 2002) The most common words are war, terror, terror, security,weapons, freedom, nation, people.
Speech by Barack Obama (25 January 2011) The dominant words are jobs, business, future, education, governance, work, people, nation.

These two speeches share common terms (people, nation, country, jobs, work), but their thematic content is clearly different: national security vs economy and education.
Two fundamental questions arise:

**How to measure this difference in a formal and quantitative way?
How to tolerate variations in style, language, vocabulary while capturing similarity of meaning?

These questions are not trivial. A “job security” document can simultaneously use the vocabulary of both speeches. A naive distance measurement (word count) is not enough to capture the semantic nuance.




The omnipresence of distance

Distance applications in data analysis
The distance (or proximity / similarity measurement) is used in all major areas of data analysis (Data Science):

Unsupervised Mining

Clustering (consolidation): group similar documents without prior labels.
Due to anomaly (Outlier Detection): identify documents that differ significantly from others.
Imputation: estimate missing values from nearest neighbours.

In clustering, two documents are placed in the same group if their distance is less than a certain threshold. The result depends entirely on the measure chosen.



Supervised Learning

Classification: assign a category to a document based on distance to training examples (e.g. k-NN).
Regression: estimate a numerical value (e.g. relevance of a document) by interpolating from neighbours.
Ranking (ranking): order documents by decreasing relevance to a query.




Visualization

Dimension Reduction (Dimension Reduction): Project high-dimensional data in a 2D or 3D space by preserving the distance between points (e.g. t-SNE, UMAP, MDS).

Visualization allows a user to navigate intuitively in a large documentary space, exploring thematic clusters.




The three roles of distance
Distance plays three distinct but complementary roles in Information Retrieval:

** Characterize a document**: the characteristics (features) of a document form its numerical “summary” — what it is in itself.
Compare two documents: distance is used to quantify the similarity between two documents — their relationship to each other.
Characterize a model of documents: the distribution of distances in a collection allows to visualize the overall structure of the corpus — how the documents are organized between them.
